messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Re: gaussian process fitting and posterior predictive distribution in stan
messages.body_plain:
You certainly can do that, but it's not going to give
you a different answer than doing it within Stan (unless there's
a bug on one side or the other).  Stan's extract function lets
you pull out the parameters for each draw in the sample.

I'm guessing from your traceplot, which shows a huge increase
in variance after adaptation, that what's happened is that the
last step of adaptation found a smaller step size and was thus
able to explore more of the posterior.  That is, the post-warmup
draws showing higher variance may be closer to the posterior
than the warmup iterations.  My suggestion would be to run
warmup for more iterations and see what the posterior looks like.

You want to inspect what happened to adaptation in the two chains you're
showing.  There's no way the posterior measures of convergence R-hat
and n_eff will look good given that traceplot with two chains of very
different means.

- Bob

won't affect the actual sampling algorithm.

It's always good to have an independent test of code.

The thing I'd be most worried about is the difference in behavior
during adaptation and sampling.  It's a sign that adaptation hadn't
fully adapted.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Formulating error in covariates logistic regression model in Stan
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Formulating error in covariates logistic regression model in Stan
messages.body_plain:
If you have discrete parameters, you need to marginalize them
out in order to sample in Stan.  There are examples in the mixture
models chapter of the manual.

It's not always feasible to do the marginalization, but if
the scope of k[i] in your example is limited to the loop body
it should be feasible.  If there are external interactions, the
combinatorics become problematic as you need to sum over K^N
elements where K is the number of possible categorical outcomes.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] cut revisited (+ mi as cut)
messages.body_plain:
On Feb 27, 2014, at 7:31 PM, Bill Gillespie <bi...@metrumrg.com> wrote:

> Dear Andrew et al,
>
> I beg your indulgence for posting a topic that is not strictly a Stan issue. I am posting it here because it follows up on an earlier thread (https://groups.google.com/forum/#!msg/stan-users/ruxPAhBPI4A/Aj-BvWGOlEQJ). In addition I am considering the use of an approach to "cut" in an analysis using Stan.

We can't resist general stats discussion, either.  Maybe
Andrew will take this up on his blog as it might be interesting
to get feedback from a wider audience and because it's connected
to the way mi uses an approach that feels just like a BUGS cut
model.

Maybe phrasing it this way will make him change his mind, but
I'd guess he'd say that he's using mi as a heuristic and he'd
do the full joint model if he could formulate the computations.
(In fact, his postdoc Yajuan (Sophie) Si did just this with non-parametric
Bayesian approaches to categorical missing data in her Duke Ph.D. thesis and
I believe is extending the work to continuous data with Andrew.)

>
> During the previous thread Andrew Gelman stated: "The reason why I (and others) perceive "cut" as bad news is because when you do "cut," you are no longer doing Bayesian inference.  To put it another way, if it's really true that you don't want inference going from A to B, I don't think you want it going from B to A either. Joint distributions go both ways."
>
> I accept that this is true for formal fully Bayesian inference, but I also think that prevention of "Bayesian feedback" is a useful heuristic in some practical contexts. David Lunn et al (Pharmacokinet Pharmacodyn (2009) 36:19–38) attempt to make that case for PKPD modeling. In that context there are usually 2 categories of dependent variable data: PK and PD, typically plasma drug concentrations and one or more measures of drug effects. In a typical PKPD model the PD outcomes are assumed to be a consequence of the PK (among other covariates).
>
> My rationale for using cut in PKPD modeling is the same (I think) as that expressed in Lunn et al. Bayesian PKPD modeling is an excellent formalism for dealing with uncertainty in the model parameters.

David Lunn and Martyn Plummer both spoke on this topic at a session during
the MCMski conference.  I didn't follow all the details, and alas, I was
the only one of the Stan team in that session.  But they might share their
slides with you if you sent them e-mail.

> However our inferences are also conditioned on the mathematical structure of our model. There is also uncertainty in the form of our model and we usually do not account for that in any formal way. In PKPD modeling there are usually 2 (or more) linked models: one for PK outcomes and one for PD outcomes where it is usually assumed that the PD outcomes are affected by the PK (but not the reverse though there are exceptions). In many cases the uncertainty in the PD submodel structure is substantially greater than that for the PK model structure. This is due in part to differences in our state of knowledge about the underlying processes that cause the observed magnitudes in PK and PD outcomes. In addition there is often interest in making inferences about both PK and PD. Given such intentions, the disparity in model uncertainty and the assumed causal path, I argue it is undesirable for the larger potential PD model misspecification to impact inferences regarding PK.
>
> I am interested in hearing other viewpoints on questions like:
> 	• Do you agree that the disparity in submodel uncertainty is an issue to be addressed in some way in the data analysis?

Absolutely!

> 	• Is the notion of "cutting feedback" from the PD data to the PK model a reasonable heuristic approach for addressing that issue, and, if not, what are the alternatives?

The amount of certainty coming from the PK model can
be addressed as a prior on the variances in the usual
Bayesian way.  This makes the joint inference consistent.
If you really are that certain about the PK estimates, then
they should have a small posterior variance and perhaps be
defined in a very narrow range of plausible support.  If they
don't, then you don't have as much certainty as you think they
do.

I think we're all a bit confused as to why those in PK/PD
think these inferences should only go one way.

> 	• Couldn't "cut" in the PKPD application be interpreted as a Bayesian analysis in which the PK model predictions are considered covariate data rather than a component of the prior? This is an attempt to argue for treating "cut" as multiple imputation of data.

If you do this, the result is not Bayesian inference on
the data being imputed.  There's also no way to implement it
in Stan or JAGS.

This is a good point.  Andrew's approach to multiple imputation is
not fully Bayesian in that it's not doing inference over a joint
probability model.

In your context, suppose we have two models:

  PK:  p(phi,y1)   params: phi,  data: y1

  PD:  p(theta,y2|phi)  params: theta,  data y2

Then doing multiple imputation on the PK posterior p(phi|y1)
by drawing a sample phi^1,...,phi^M and
and then plugging that into the PD model to compute

  p(theta) =?= INT p(theta|y2,phi) p(phi|y1) d.phi

           =approx= SUM_m p(theta | y2, phi^m)

will not yield the same inferences as the joint PK/PD model

  PK/PD:   p(phi,theta,y1,y2) = p(theta,y2|phi) * p(phi,y1)

specifically because of the way phi is "cut".

Now I'm curious as to what Andrew will say about multiple imputation,
because it suffers exactly the same defect w.r.t. full Bayes.

Or what other PK/PD modelers will say, because we've heard this
request before in exactly this context ("we trust our PK more
than our PD so want to cut the PK inferences from the PD inferences").

For instance, what happens when you do the joint inference?  Do you
get results that are completely implausible?  Maybe that says that
the PD model is just not right rather than that you shouldn't be doing
joint inference.

- Bob

> So the bottom line is that I am trying to make the case for "cut", or to provoke someone into setting me straight.
>
> I should also mention that I am aware of Martyn Plummer's convincing criticism of the approach to "cut" used in BUGS (http://www.pages.drexel.edu/~mwl25/mcmski/slides/mp_cuts.pdf), so I am not arguing for that approach. Instead I plan to apply the multiple imputation approach he suggests.
>
> Thanks,
> Bill
>

Hi all.  I was corresponding with someone who was trying to use Stan for models with discrete parameters, using the mixture model formulation as explained in the manual.  He felt that the log-probability specification was hard for users in his subfield to understand.  This made me think, maybe we could add a new distribution called finite_mixture or something like that, where the arguments are the probabilities and the mixture distributions. I’m not quite sure how this would be done—to do it in sufficient generality to be useful might end up being even more complicated to use—but I just wanted to throw this idea out there.

On Mar 1, 2014, at 7:16 PM, Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:

> Hi all.  I was corresponding with someone who was trying to use Stan for models with discrete parameters, using the mixture model formulation as explained in the manual.  He felt that the log-probability specification was hard for users in his subfield to understand.  This made me think, maybe we could add a new distribution called finite_mixture or something like that, where the arguments are the probabilities and the mixture distributions. I'm not quite sure how this would be done--to do it in sufficient generality to be useful might end up being even more complicated to use--but I just wanted to throw this idea out there.

I added an issue to which you (or others) can comment on GitHub:

  https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/583

I can't quite tell what you're thinking of in terms of a concrete
syntax.  Something like a distribution:

  y ~ finite_mixture(lambda,
                     normal(mu1,sigma1),
                     normal(mu2,sigma2),
                     normal(mu3,sigma3));

for a three-way mixture where lambda is a 3-simplex and so on?
Or something more like a function, as in:

  increment_log_prob(finite_mixture(lambda,
                                    normal_log(y,mu1,sigma1),
                                    normal_log(y,mu2,sigma2),
                                    normal_log(y,mu3,sigma3)));

We can be pretty flexible with things in the modeling language,
so that we could take any number of arguments for something like
this.

But I've been having a hard time seeing how we could parameterize
all this.  Especially if we have vector parmaeters y, mu or sigma.

Mixtures aren't the only case we want to deal with when marginalizing
out discrete params, but we could perhaps start there.

And what's the priority for this, if any?  You've told me recently not
to bother with adding new distributions and to let users do it, but
this is going to be much trickier because it's not a usual function
or distribution but something that needs to be finessed in the
modeling language for a flexible syntax.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
I think that's a challenge to explain increment_log_prob()
and the way Stan works more clearly.

There are three confusing aspects:

1.  The sampling notation ~ doesn't literally sample the left
side from the distribution on the right --- it just increments
the log probability.

2.  Suffixing "_log" to a distribution name gives you a function.

3.  The function doesn't drop constant terms and the sampling
notation version does.

All three points have led to a great deal of confusion.

One thing I'd like to do is have a version of the "_log"-suffixed
functions that does drop constant terms, so I can say something like:

   y ~ normal(mu,sigma);

is equivalent to:

  increment_log_prob(normal_log_propto(y,mu,sigma));

- Bob

I think, in retrospect, it may have been a mistake to make the syntax the same as BUGS when what it means is very different from what BUGS means. In my class, we are learning Stan before BUGS, so we'll see if the students get confused the other way..

> 2.  Suffixing "_log" to a distribution name gives you a function.

This is pretty straightforward I think if you understand point 1, which is to say that you understand that Stan is not a Gibbs sampler and need to work with PDFs of distributions rather than merely PRNGs for distributions.

> 3.  The function doesn't drop constant terms and the sampling
> notation version does.

This is big-time confusing, particularly because people need the constants sometimes. I still think it would be relatively easy to have Stan calculate the log posterior once with constants included, once with constants excluded, cache the difference, and then initialize the quantity formerly known as lp__ to that in subsequent iterations. That way, we don't waste (much) time calculating constants but we remove the inconsistency in the output. Then we just have to remind people of the hidden Jacobian terms.

Ben

messages.subject: sampling syntax vs. increment_log_prob
messages.body_plain:
[changed subject]

"Leaky" sounds like a bad thing!  I see the term derives
from Joel Spolsky, who has a knack for catchy naming:

  http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leaky_abstraction

I like to think of the abstraction here as being that
the model defines a log probability function over
parameters up to a constant.  As such, I view the
sampling statements not so much as an abstraction as
syntactic sugar for the direct increment.

  http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syntactic_sugar

Stan's given users the ability to manipulate lp__ from the
beginning.  That's been deprecated and hidden behind
increment_log_prob() and sampling statement syntax, both
of which do provide a layer of abstraction over manipulating
the log probability accumulator lp__ directly.

- Bob

On Mar 1, 2014, at 9:20 PM, Ben Goodrich <goodri...@gmail.com> wrote:

> On Saturday, March 1, 2014 3:13:38 PM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> I think that's a challenge to explain increment_log_prob()
> and the way Stan works more clearly.
>
> There are three confusing aspects:
>
> 1.  The sampling notation ~ doesn't literally sample the left
> side from the distribution on the right --- it just increments
> the log probability.
>
> I think, in retrospect, it may have been a mistake to make the syntax the same as BUGS when what it means is very different from what BUGS means. In my class, we are learning Stan before BUGS, so we'll see if the students get confused the other way..

But BUGS doesn't mean direct sampling either!

In BUGS/JAGS, the sampling statements and assignments define
(roughly) a directed acyclic graph.  And then the Markov blanket
of a node lets you define conditional distribution for it with which
you can do Gibbs sampling (or an approximation thereof, like slice
sampling):

  http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Markov_blanket

> 2.  Suffixing "_log" to a distribution name gives you a function.
>
> This is pretty straightforward I think if you understand point 1, which is to say that you understand that Stan is not a Gibbs sampler and need to work with PDFs of distributions rather than merely PRNGs for distributions.

I don't think anyone can get by with PRNGs only, unless they
want to build a big and inefficient rejection sampler!

Languages like Church have an interesting take on this where
the equivalent of the sampling statements in BUGS or Stan
are kind of like direct statements, but also kind of not like
them because they do something like Metropolis over execution
paths (in a way I still don't fully comprehend --- if someone has
a pointer to an explanation of how sampling actually works in Church,
please post it).

> 3.  The function doesn't drop constant terms and the sampling
> notation version does.
>
> This is big-time confusing, particularly because people need the constants sometimes. I still think it would be relatively easy to have Stan calculate the log posterior once with constants included, once with constants excluded, cache the difference, and then initialize the quantity formerly known as lp__ to that in subsequent iterations. That way, we don't waste (much) time calculating constants but we remove the inconsistency in the output. Then we just have to remind people of the hidden Jacobian terms.

That's a great idea and there's no way to do it efficiently
direclty within Stan as it is.  Had we been more concerned with model comparison
at the get go, we probably would've built that in.

No reason we can't do that now, so I created an issue for it:

  https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/584

- Bob

The way it was explained to me was that you translate
the posterior evaluation into an expression graph where
each evaluation is a random function.  So instead of
assigning a node to, say, f(x), it gets the random value
f ~ pi(x).  Then you can resample by selecting a node,
resampling a value, and propagating that down the graph
resampling until you hit the end of the graph.

The values at the end are then used as a Metropolis proposal
to compensate for any approximate sampling used instead
of exact sampling.

See the discussion at
http://blog.codinghorror.com/all-abstractions-are-failed-abstractions/
especially this bit:

  Instead, let's ask ourselves a more pragmatic question: Does this
  abstraction make our code at least a little easier to write? To
  understand? To troubleshoot? Are we better off with this abstraction
  than we were without it?

Stan is a DSL (domain-specific language), and a particularly good
one. The ~ abstraction is very useful in this problem domain
(statistics), because it allows us to say what we mean. I see no major
problem with it being a bit "leaky".

That said, I think that the biggest leak is when one needs to manually
correct for Jacobians. But it is reasonable to assume that users of Stan
have some training in basic probability (no need to be a statistician,
just having taken an more or less advanced undergrad course is enough
IMO) so as long as we can't come up with a more abstract solution for
this it is fine.

Best,

Tamas

messages.body_plain:
On Mar 2, 2014, at 12:01 PM, Tamas Papp <tkp...@gmail.com> wrote:

> ...

> That said, I think that the biggest leak is when one needs to manually
> correct for Jacobians. But it is reasonable to assume that users of Stan
> have some training in basic probability (no need to be a statistician,
> just having taken an more or less advanced undergrad course is enough
> IMO) so as long as we can't come up with a more abstract solution for
> this it is fine.

Setting aside the semantics of what the "abstraction" is and whether
it is "leaky" or not, we could mitigate the problem of having to specify
Jacobians by exposing a class of transform functions that automatically
compute and apply the Jacobian.  That's what our constrained variables
already do.  In order to make it clean, we'd have to allow it to be used
in transformed data and generated quantities blocks that do not require
Jacobians by just skipping that part of the transform.

The syntax of allowing expressions on the left-hand side of sampling
statements could be restricted to just variables or constants, as BUGS/JAGS
do, and that would in some sense "plug the leak" by reducing the expressiveness
of the language.  I don't think BUGS or JAGS let you do this if x is a parameter:

   y <- log(x)
   y ~ normal(mu,sigma)

because you wind up having two parents for the node y.

I think the "leakiest" part of Stan's sampling abstraction is that "~" can only be
used in the model (it could potentially be used in transformed parameters, but
we decided to disallow it thinking it would be clearer restricted to the model).
The "leaky" part of the function abstraction is that (P)RNG functions can only be used
in generated quantities.  These restrictions respectively makes the statements and
expressions context-dependent in their use.

The really really big "leak" is that we can't use integers as parameters.
Because we allow general log probability computations, it's impossible to pull
out the Markov blanket of a parameter.

- Bob

> it is "leaky" or not, we could mitigate the problem of having to specify
> Jacobians by exposing a class of transform functions that automatically
> compute and apply the Jacobian.  That's what our constrained variables
> already do.  In order to make it clean, we'd have to allow it to be used
> in transformed data and generated quantities blocks that do not require
> Jacobians by just skipping that part of the transform.

Why should this functionality be restricted to a class of transform
functions? I guess all bijections could be supported.

> The syntax of allowing expressions on the left-hand side of sampling
> statements could be restricted to just variables or constants, as BUGS/JAGS
> do, and that would in some sense "plug the leak" by reducing the expressiveness
> of the language.  I don't think BUGS or JAGS let you do this if x is a parameter:
>
>    y <- log(x)
>    y ~ normal(mu,sigma)
>
> because you wind up having two parents for the node y.

I could imagine a different syntax for a transformation, eg some
character that is not used for anything else but is different from <-
and ~. Let's imagine for a moment that it's, say, \, then

y \ log(x)

would mean "adjust the posterior according to the Jacobian correction."

> I think the "leakiest" part of Stan's sampling abstraction is that "~" can only be
> used in the model (it could potentially be used in transformed parameters, but
> we decided to disallow it thinking it would be clearer restricted to the model).
> The "leaky" part of the function abstraction is that (P)RNG functions can only be used
> in generated quantities.  These restrictions respectively makes the statements and
> expressions context-dependent in their use.

I imagine that in the long run Stan could be organized into layers: the
bottom layer would simply be an engine for specifying a function (the
posterior), with some bare syntax (eg an enumeration of terms that need
to be added to it, no ~, no Jacobians, etc), then layers on top of that
could implement convenience forms (eg ~, Jacobians) that transform into
bottom layer code. Users would rarely ever need to see the bottom layer
for simple code (much like manipulations of lp__ are rarely needed in
simple cases).

I expect that this approach would benefit a lot from Stan being a
declarative/functional language, instead of the current
declarative/imperative mix. I am not familiar with the details of the
implementation, but I am wondering if re-assigning variables really buys
anything in terms of speed or ease of implementation.

> The really really big "leak" is that we can't use integers as parameters.
> Because we allow general log probability computations, it's impossible to pull
> out the Markov blanket of a parameter.

I think that this is something orthogonal to the issue we discussed in
this thread, but maybe I misunderstand.

Best,

Tamas

the three phases (upswing, meta-equilibrium, downswing) then you could fit the model as

Then the cut points can be computed as the locations where one component rises past
another (computable analytically for many possible shapes).

Not sure how easy it would be to model those shapes, but it seems more informative than
fitting with a non-parameteric model and simply looking for the changes in derivative.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] sampling syntax vs. increment_log_prob
messages.body_plain:
Thanks for the suggestions.

I agree that it'd make sense to call out the Jacobian adjustment
if it happens.  It's definitely in the "advanced" category --- I
was using BUGS happily before I even understood what a Jacobian was.

To clarify, Stan is 100% imperative.  The sampling statements may
appear to be declarative, but they're purely imperative --- they just
increment the log probabilty function and are executed imperatively in
the order they are found.

There's are presently no functional components to Stan --- nothing
where you can pass a function to another function or in any way treat
functions as first-class objects.

You're right --- not being able to sample integers is orthogonal
to sampling statements vs. increment_log_prob statements.

- Bob

On Mar 2, 2014, at 6:20 PM, Tamas Papp <tkp...@gmail.com> wrote:

> On Sun, Mar 02 2014, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
>
>> On Mar 2, 2014, at 12:01 PM, Tamas Papp <tkp...@gmail.com> wrote:
>>
>>> ...
>>> That said, I think that the biggest leak is when one needs to manually
>>> correct for Jacobians. But it is reasonable to assume that users of Stan
>>> have some training in basic probability (no need to be a statistician,
>>> just having taken an more or less advanced undergrad course is enough
>>> IMO) so as long as we can't come up with a more abstract solution for
>>> this it is fine.
>>
>> Setting aside the semantics of what the "abstraction" is and whether
>> it is "leaky" or not, we could mitigate the problem of having to specify
>> Jacobians by exposing a class of transform functions that automatically
>> compute and apply the Jacobian.  That's what our constrained variables
>> already do.  In order to make it clean, we'd have to allow it to be used
>> in transformed data and generated quantities blocks that do not require
>> Jacobians by just skipping that part of the transform.
>
> Why should this functionality be restricted to a class of transform
> functions? I guess all bijections could be supported.
>
>> The syntax of allowing expressions on the left-hand side of sampling
>> statements could be restricted to just variables or constants, as BUGS/JAGS
>> do, and that would in some sense "plug the leak" by reducing the expressiveness
>> of the language.  I don't think BUGS or JAGS let you do this if x is a parameter:
>>
>>   y <- log(x)
>>   y ~ normal(mu,sigma)
>>
>> because you wind up having two parents for the node y.
>
> I could imagine a different syntax for a transformation, eg some
> character that is not used for anything else but is different from <-
> and ~. Let's imagine for a moment that it's, say, \, then
>
> y \ log(x)
>
> would mean "adjust the posterior according to the Jacobian correction."
>
>> I think the "leakiest" part of Stan's sampling abstraction is that "~" can only be
>> used in the model (it could potentially be used in transformed parameters, but
>> we decided to disallow it thinking it would be clearer restricted to the model).
>> The "leaky" part of the function abstraction is that (P)RNG functions can only be used
>> in generated quantities.  These restrictions respectively makes the statements and
>> expressions context-dependent in their use.
>
> I imagine that in the long run Stan could be organized into layers: the
> bottom layer would simply be an engine for specifying a function (the
> posterior), with some bare syntax (eg an enumeration of terms that need
> to be added to it, no ~, no Jacobians, etc), then layers on top of that
> could implement convenience forms (eg ~, Jacobians) that transform into
> bottom layer code. Users would rarely ever need to see the bottom layer
> for simple code (much like manipulations of lp__ are rarely needed in
> simple cases).
>
> I expect that this approach would benefit a lot from Stan being a
> declarative/functional language, instead of the current
> declarative/imperative mix. I am not familiar with the details of the
> implementation, but I am wondering if re-assigning variables really buys
> anything in terms of speed or ease of implementation.
>
>> The really really big "leak" is that we can't use integers as parameters.
>> Because we allow general log probability computations, it's impossible to pull
>> out the Markov blanket of a parameter.
>
> I think that this is something orthogonal to the issue we discussed in
> this thread, but maybe I misunderstand.
>
> Best,
>
> Tamas
>

two are easily confounded.

I meant another aspect of functional languages: immutable values (think
Haskell, not CL).

Tamas

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] sampling syntax vs. increment_log_prob
messages.body_plain:
On Mar 2, 2014, at 9:11 PM, Tamas Papp <tkp...@gmail.com> wrote:

> I think that there is an important distinction here:
> STAN-the-implementation is clearly imperative, but STAN-the-language
> contains elements (the ~ statements) that could be understood as
> declarative (even if their implementation is imperative). Currently
> there is a single implementation (which of course makes sense), so the
> two are easily confounded.

I hadn't even thought of different implementations.  If
you removed the assignment statements and increment_log_prob, you
could be left with something that's roughly declarative in the
same sense as BUGS/JAGS.  In fact, that's where I started the design.
There are a lot of advantages in terms of static program analysis
(as in ML, to add another functional language to the mix).

I think a good comparison is Prolog, which masquerades as
declarative, but is in fact imperative due to the depth-first
execution order.  The order of those clauses really matters,
and that's not even considering cut (! operation, not to be confused
with cut in BUGS).

> I meant another aspect of functional languages: immutable values (think
> Haskell, not CL).

Took me a while to figure out "CL" meant "Common Lisp".

The parameters and data are immutable, whereas transformed data,
transformed parameters, generated quantities, loop indices,
and local variables are all mutable (not sure having loop indices
be mutable in their bodies is really useful, though).

Maybe with inline declarations and compound declaration-definition
statements we could make everything but local variables immutable.

I'm a huge fan of immutables in coding, by the way --- I argued
at length for them in Java and have been pretty insistent that
our C++ uses immutable classes wherever possible rather than
construct-empty then apply setters.  I like to be able to validate
that objects are well formed on construction and then make sure
they stay that way.

- Bob

P.S.  "Stan" isn't an acronym --- no need to capitalize.  I think
      our all-caps logo is confusing it's not-an-acronym status, as
      is Andrew's jumping in with ridiculous "bacronyms".

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] sampling syntax vs. increment_log_prob
messages.body_plain:
> When I say a proper language, I mean conceptually thinking of the code
> in a Stan model block as a deterministic program which produces one
> sample.

This is a bit oxymoronic, no?  If we wanted to generate a sample (transition, whatever
you want to call it) then the code would have to be stochastic.

In any case, the model block really just defines a probability density, with
the distinction from a many-to-one function f : R^{n} -> R coming from the
need for Jacobians.  This is how it works right now and how I believe it
should continue to work in the future — I’m not convinced of the utility
of trying to abstract this away to anything else.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] sampling syntax vs. increment_log_prob
messages.body_plain:
Thanks for the clarification.  I see what you mean now.

One reason I think of Stan as more of a language for defining
a log probability function is that we also use it for optimization
and are working on marginal maximal likelihood, EP and VB inference
(all of which are deterministic modulo initialization).

We're also working toward more finely articulating the log probability
function itself, such as splitting out the likelihood from the prior,
so that we can define WAIC (a nicer alternative to DIC) and splitting
up the data into batches so that we can use stochastic and parallel
inferences of various sorts.

- Bob

That could be an interesting solution. So far, I've gone rather brute-force, just testing all combinations of switchpoints and returning the best fit. I'm forcing the gradient of the middle segment to be zero; otherwise, it decides the first line segment has length 1 and is therefore able to perfectly match the first two data points, which returns a perfect score for that segment. By making the assumption that there's a zero in between, I get a reasonable fit ( see attached image ).

I'll see what I can come up with with your idea, Michael. Thanks again.

messages.body_plain:
Cool.  The other advantage with an approach like this is that you can put lots of science into the model, for example modeling an epidemic with a Gaussian or a Laplacian and then modeling with a mixture of two of these guys and a uniform between them.
In fact, if you assumed that data collection started in the midst of one epidemic and ended in the midst of another your model would be two exponentials decaying from the boundaries and uniform in between, very similar to the simple piecewise linear
model you have used here.

Good luck!

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] priors when using cholesky_decomposition
messages.body_plain:
We recommend using a correlation matrix, and having a uniform
distribution on it is well-defined.  The lkj_corr(2.0) regularizes
a bit toward the identity correlation matrix.  Indeed it's slower
because it requires more work.  We have some plans in place to
add a cholesky_factor_corr type --- it's just waiting for transforms
to be added.

There's not an easy way yet to put a prior on the Cholesky factor
directly because of the required Jacobian, but we are going to add
the LKJ version of that, too.  Ben can explain how it works.

For speed and size of output, you don't need to make the cov_matrix
transformed parameters --- you can make them local variables in the model
and they won't be printed.  We've usually found it easier to look at the
correlation matrices and scales anyway.

Your deviance won't be the total deviance because you're missing
the multi_normal_cholesky terms.

You can just increment_log_prob(log_lik0), which is already the
sum of the log_lik.  Not repeating sub-calculations is always
faster.

Also, this should all get faster if we ever get around to vectorizing
the multi_normal, which we really should be doing for this kind of model.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Transdimensional MCMC for model comparison in Stan
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Transdimensional MCMC for model comparison in Stan
messages.body_plain:
Reasonable initializations always help.  And you should always run
models until everything converges, or fix the models so that they do.

Initializing a mixture with individual fits is not usually a reasonable
estimate of the mixture itself.  For instance, if you mix two normals,
they'll both be initialized to the same fit, which is not where they'll go
in the mixture itself.

What can happen in mixtures is that one component will dominate and
the other will be harder to estimate.   This should be less problematic
in Stan because we're marginalizing out the mixture ratio than in
a Gibbs sampler for the discrete responsibility parameter.

Or to take the normal again, it's hard to fit a normal mixture to data that's
really unimodal normal.  The components aren't well distinguished from one
another and the degenerate solution of assigning all weight to one component should
win out.  Priors on the mixing ratio can help prevent this problem.

What is the mixture ratio you're fitting?

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] priors when using cholesky_decomposition
messages.body_plain:
The default is a uniform distribution over all correlation
matrices (positive definite, values bounded between -1 and 1).
Because correlation matrices have bounded values, the uniform distribution
is proper.

There's no way to directly place bounds other than (-1,1) on the
correlations.  But they're not all free to vary between -1 and 1
because positive-definitenes must be maintained.

No, we don't have a time for vectorizing multi-normal.  Hopefully
we'll get it done by the end of the summer.  It really shouldn't
be too much work to at least do the simple cases allowing an array
of outcomes, which is where the speed bump will come from.
I've added a high-priority feature request for this because we really
should have it in place and it's not that hard:

  http://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/589

To answer your other question, if you want the full log likelihood of
the model, you're not including the contribution of the multi_normal_cholesky
terms in the model.  If they're only being used to generate predictive
quantities, that's OK.  What we also need to do is add the _rng function
for multi_normal_cholesky, and then they could be moved to the generated
quantities block.  Hence, another issue:

  https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/590

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Sorry --- didn't read your model that closely.  I see that
you have both

    log_lik[i] <- multi_normal_cholesky_log(y[i],mu[i],Ly);}

and

    y[i] ~ multi_normal_cholesky(mu[i], Ly);

This is doing redundant work.  You can either

1.  add

    increment_log_prob(sum(log_lik));

    to the model and remove the y[i] ~ ...

or

2.  Calculate log_lik in the generated quantities block.

Andrew prefers (2) in order to keep the calculation of WAIC
separate from the model and for efficiency.

We're in the middle of writing up some recommendations on
WAIC calculations, which we'll share when they're done.

- Bob

Not at the moment. We are currently refactoring Stan, CmdStan, and RStan simultaneously. You're not going to be able to do it easily from the develop branch of RStan.

There is, however, a branch I'm working on that is experimental and is up to date with the current version of Stan. It's feature/refactor_stan_command.

> I see that the main stan repo is downloaded when you clone the rstan repo and I was wondering if there was a simple way to change that hook to the newest version (or if it would be possible to add one like that to the rstan repo).

That isn't true. Stan is a submodule inside RStan. It does not get downloaded automatically.

There are easy ways to change the submodule version. Read up on git submodules to find out how to use them. (They're tricky, but not impossible and it's beyond the scope of our users list to discuss how to use git.)

messages.subject_clean: How to write a nonstandard prior in Stan?
messages.body_snippet:
I have a standard logistic regression model, with two predictors. So I have beta0, beta1 and beta2, each have a Normal prior.

Then I calculate p[i] <- inv_logit(beta0 + beta1 * x1[i] + beta2 * x2[i])

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] How to write a nonstandard prior in Stan?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] How to write a nonstandard prior in Stan?
messages.body_plain:
With the binomial formulation, the lambda[i] are independent
and you could just drop them altogether replace the step function with
a comparison, and write

  (p[i] > 0.5) ~ bernoulli(theta);

You could even remove the inv_logit for p[i] and compare on the logit
scale:

  for (i in 1:N)
    (beta0 + beta1 * x1[i] + beta2 * x2[i] > logit(0.5)) ~ bernoulli(theta);

And you don't technically need a Jacobian here, but ...

Your bigger problem is that it's a non-continuous prior,
which HMC isn't really designed to handle.  I doubt Gibbs will mix
any better.  The samples will not mix well, especially if there are
a lot of cases near the boundary.  And you may wind up with posterior
modes (my intuition's not good here as to what this prior's doing).

But I wouldn't recommend it.  Reformulating the prior as something
continuous would be better, such as a prior on the expected number
of successes, which is just sum(p) in your formulation.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Understanding bad performance
messages.body_plain:
Here are some stats for the latest run on this model.

For lp__, N_Eff / N = 0.0019.

 Of the 13,886 parameters,

* 75.6% (10,492) have N_Eff / N = 1

* 24.2% (3,355) have N_Eff / N in the range [0.1, 1)

* 0.27% (38) have N_Eff / N in the range [0.01, 0.1)

* One has N_Eff / N == 0.0039.

treedepth__ is usually 9 after warmup. During warmup it usually ranges between 8 and 11.

The three chains took 15.8, 21.7, and 12.9 seconds per iteration during warmup. They took 11.1, 10.2, and 6.2 seconds per iteration during sampling.

This is a multinomial probit model with a full covariance matrix, used for analyzing survey data. Each of the survey responses is Likert scale (ordinal), and has a corresponding continuous latent variable. The observed responses are derived from the latent responses via a vector of cutpoints, plus two individual-level scale-usage parameters that scale and translate the cutpoint vector. The scale-usage parameters have a hierarchical structure.

The constraints are the data: each latent response must lie between an upper and lower bound determined by the ordinal response. This is actually implemented by having parameters constrained to lie between 0 and 1, and then obtaining the latent responses as transformed parameters by scaling and translating.

messages.body_plain:
I'm not sure this has anything to do with the problem, but I think the definition of the NB as listed in the manual is incorrect, unless a different parameterization is being used.

I believe the combinatorial prefix should be:
Choose(n + a - 1, a)

instead of:
Choose(n + a - 1, a - 1)

Thus, the logs should be:
lgamma(a + n) - lgmma(a + 1) - lgamma(n)

instead of:
lgamma(a + n) - lgmma(n + 1) - lgamma(a)

and the errors propagate to the gradient definitions.

If this is what is being programmed, that may be the source of some issues.

Avi

messages.body_plain:
On further review, it may well be that this could be due to R and Stan using different parameterizations. If Stan is actually following Gelman et al (2014 p. 44), then it is self consistent, but has defined successes and failures opposite that of R (check ?rbinom). Stan seems to be using alpha is the number of set failures for which we are finding the probability of y successes. R, on the other hand, has x as the random successes before a fixed number of n failures. In other words, "p" and (1-p) are reversed so that the exponent to the 1 / 1+ b and b / 1 + b have to be switched between the two.

Compare Wikipedia <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Negative_binomial_distribution#Gamma.E2.80.93Poisson_mixture> with Wolfram <http://mathworld.wolfram.com/NegativeBinomialDistribution.html> for an example where the exponents are "swapped" because of the definitions.

On Mar 7, 2014, at 8:07 PM, Avraham Adler <avraha...@gmail.com> wrote:

> On further review, it may well be that this could be due to R and Stan using different parameterizations. If Stan is actually following Gelman et al (2014 p. 44), then it is self consistent, but has defined successes and failures opposite that of R (check ?rbinom). Stan is using the same formulation as found in Wikipedia, in that alpha is the number of set failures for which we are finding the probability of y successes. R, on the other hand, has x as the random successes before a fixed number of n failures. In other words, "p" and (1-p) are reversed so that the exponent to the 1 / 1+ b and b / 1 + b have to be switched between the two.
>
> Linus, using your Stan parametrization, did you generate variates in R using size and mu?
>
>

> I'm not sure this has anything to do with the problem, but I think the definition of the NB as listed in the manual is incorrect, unless a different parameterization is being used.
>
> I believe the combinatorial prefix should be:
> Choose(n + a - 1, a)
>
> instead of:
> Choose(n + a - 1, a - 1)
>
> Thus, the logs should be:
> lgamma(a + n) - lgmma(a + 1) - lgamma(n)
>
> instead of:
> lgamma(a + n) - lgmma(n + 1) - lgamma(a)
>
> and the errors propagate to the gradient definitions.
>
> If this is what is being programmed, that may be the source of some issues.
>
> Avi

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] issue with neg_binomial_rng
messages.body_plain:
Here's a minimal reproducible example:

     require(rstan)
     fit <- stan(model_code=
     'data {
       real shape;
       real mu;
     }
     parameters {
       real any; //just a dummy to make this compile
     }
     model {
       any ~ normal(0, 1);
     }
     generated quantities {
       real y_correct[1000];
       real y_incorrect[1000];

       for (i in 1:1000) {
         y_correct [i] <- poisson_rng (gamma_rng (shape, shape/mu));
       }

       for (i in 1:1000) {
         y_incorrect [i] <- neg_binomial_rng(shape, shape/mu);
       }
     }', data=list(shape=4, mu=2))

     as.matrix(fit) -> mfit
     correct_sample <- mfit[, grep("y_correct", colnames(mfit))]
     incorrect_sample <- mfit[, grep("y_incorrect", colnames(mfit))]

     r_test <- rnbinom(1000, mu=2, size=4)

     mean(correct_sample)
     mean(incorrect_sample)
     mean(r_test)
     sd(correct_sample)
     sd(incorrect_sample)
     sd(r_test)

messages.body_plain:
On Mar 7, 2014, at 6:01 PM, Avraham Adler <avraha...@gmail.com> wrote:

>
> In a recent thread about the syntax of Stan as a language, Bob made the following statement about WAIC:
>
> We're also working toward more finely articulating the log probability
> function itself, such as splitting out the likelihood from the prior,
> so that we can define WAIC (a nicer alternative to DIC) and splitting
> up the data into batches so that we can use stochastic and parallel
> inferences of various sorts.
>
> What exactly is meant by "splitting the likelihood from the prior?"

Just having ways to label the components of a model.  Perhaps having
them computed in their own blocks.  That still won't necessarily solve
the problem of needing the individual likelihoods for each data item
needed for WAIC.

> From the way I understood WAIC as defined in Gelman et al. (2014, pp. 173–174), one can calculate the WAIC using Stan in the following way:
> 	• In the generated quantities block, capture the likelihood at each point individually for every collected sample (for loop onto a vector, for example)
> 	• Once the sampling is done, calculate:
> 		• The log of the pointwise mean likelihoods [2.1]
> 		• The sample variance of the logs of the point-wise likelihoods (pWAIC2) [2.2]
> 	• Calculate -2 * {sum ([2.1]) - sum([2.2])}
> Was all that was meant that instead of manually capturing the point-wise likelihoods (which, for the built-in distributions need exponentiation as only log-densities are defined) there will be an option to block collect them, or am I exhibiting a deeper misunderstanding of the process.

Right --- that's all I meant.  But we're not sure we're going to do
it this way because the capture in generated quantities is going to be
more efficient.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Sorry for the cryptic warning --- we need to do a better job of
saying exactly which parameter is causing problems.

I'm guessing the problem here (as indicating by your print) is
that you have values pushing up against boundaries.  This will
cause numerical instabilities due to overflow or underflow in
the transforms.

The cryptic message comes about because the transform yields
a not-a-number value (NaN), and NaN is not > 0.  The only
values getting transformed are the parameters --- everything
else happens inside code corresponding to the statements in
the transformed parameter or model blocks.

I'd suggest working on the log scale and vectorizing.

We have functions

  log_inv_logit(u) = log(inv_logit(u))

and

  log1m_inv_logit(u) = log(1 - inv_logit(u))

and a log-scale Poisson

  poisson_log(y|alpha) =def= poisson(y|exp(alpha))

for just this reason.

Here's the rewritten model:

data {
  int N;        // number of length classes
  int y1[N];    // number counted in codend
  int y2[N];    // number counted in cover

  vector[2] q;    // sampling fracions of (cover, codend)
  vector[N] len;  // length classes

}

parameters {
  real<lower=0> l50;       // length of 50% retention probability
  real<lower=0> SR;        // 75% selection range

  vector[N] log_lambda;     // log of unknown total number of fish caught per lengthclass
}

transformed parameters {
  vector[N] log_p;  // log retention probability
  vector[N] log1m_p;  // log 1 - retention prob
  vector[N] theta;    // linear function of l50/SR/length

  theta <- 2 * (log(3) / SR) * (len - l50);

  for (i in 1:N) {

    log_p[i] <- log_inv_logit(theta[i]);
    log1m_p[i] <- log1m_inv_logit(theta[i]);

  }
}

model {
  l50 ~ lognormal(0, 10);
  SR ~ lognormal(0, 10);

  log_lambda ~ normal(0,100);

  y1 ~ poisson_log(log(q[1]) + log_p + log_lambda);
  y2 ~ poisson_log(log(q[2]) + log1m_p + log_lambda);
}

messages.subject: Asymmetric Laplace distribution
messages.body_plain:
Dear stan users,

I wonder if the asymmetric Laplace distribution can be implemented in stan. It is a generalization of the Laplace distribution (this one is implemented). My motivation is to use Bayesian quantile regression which is directly related with the asymmetric Laplace distribution (Yu and Moyeed, 2001). If it is possible, what should I do?

The reference that links quantile regression with the asymmetric Laplace distribution:

Cheers,
L

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Asymmetric Laplace distribution
messages.body_plain:
Hi Leo,

You can always implement the distribution directly in the model. (The syntax may be a little easier once we have functions in the language, but you can do it now without much of a problem.)

So, inside your model block, you can do something like (for the normal distribution):

model {
   increment_log_prob( ... );
}

where ... is the expression for the log of the probability distribution. By coding it this way, you'll be able to allow either y, mu, sigma, or p to be declared as parameters (jointly, even) without having to figure out the gradients with respect to each of the arguments.

It looks like the gradient is going to be undefined right at y == mu, but it doesn't look like it's going to be a problem.

If you want to create a formal request to add it, feel free to use our issue tracker at:
https://github.com/stan-dev/stan

It would help if you provided the expression for the pdf there (looks like there isn't a "standard" parameterization of this thing yet). And if you had gradients on hand for each of the arguments, that would help too.

Daniel

messages.body_plain:
Right --- 0^x is non-zero by convention for convenience in
some places.  In the C++ lib, it's unspecified behavior
that's implementation dependent:

  http://www.cplusplus.com/reference/cmath/pow/

but is allowed to raise an error.

What Stan actually does for the probability functions is work
on the log scale, so it's

  log(0^x) = x log(0) = x * -inf, which is either +/- inf

depending on the sign of x, and when converted back to the
linear scale is either 0 or inf, as you say.

We should definitely specify the behavior for beta(y|alpha,beta)
in these cases --- I don't think it makes sense to follow the
convention and have infinite density --- we should be raising an
exception.

- Bob

The prospect of incrementing lp__ by hand (or through increment_log_prob) scares me a bit, so I'd like guidance on the right way to proceed without breaking anything.  And the manual should be updated to incorporate those same fixes.

Thanks,
Josh

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Compiler warning when using manual example
messages.body_plain:
That's a false positive from the parser, and I'm not
seeing it in v2.2.0's parser, at least through RStan.

But I just updated the conditions for this warning extensively
for the next release to remove false positives from linear transforms.
You only need a Jacobian adjustment for a non-linear transform, and
we were spitting out far too many false-positive warnings.

The error would've been from another statement, anway, because it's
only triggered on sampling statements.

The comment on Omega needs to be changed because it's the prior
correlation, not covariance.  And note on the next page of the manual
that it's more efficient to use diag_pre_multiply() and diag_post_multiply().
I noted the comment udate at:

  https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/567

- Bob

> > Hi Folks -
> >
> > I'm hoping to use Stan to estimate a model in which I would historically have included an integer-valued latent variable, and was wondering if the approach I'm hoping to use would break the gradient for HMC sufficiently to make it more worthwhile to use a sampler that explicitly deals with integer-valued latent variables.
> >
> > So, I have a dataset on pediatric hospital admissions from 3 large hospitals and am trying to estimate age-specific rates of diarrheal disease risk for children < 5 years old as a function of social and environmental covariates. I'm hoping to model the counts for each age/week using a Poisson log-linear model.
> >

messages.body_plain:
Hi Bob,

I realized some issues with stanc output in visual studio compilation.

1. missing #include"stdAfx.h"
This can be simply fixed by adding new function to do it.

I simply added new function in src/stan/gm/generator.hpp

>     void generate_include_custom(const std::string& lib_name, std::ostream& o) {
>       o << "#include" << " " << "\"" << lib_name << "\"" << EOL;
>     }

and add the following code in "void generate_includes(std::ostream& o)" in the same source code

>       #ifdef WIN32
>          generate_include_custom("stdafx.h",o);
>       #endif

in front of "generate_include("stan/model/model_header.hpp",o);"

2. compilation error of stanc outputs
I am not sure this is a bug (in visual studio) or not, but the output of stanc must be modified accordingly to avoid an error in visual studio.

I used the bernoulli example here, too. In the generated cpp file, there is lines(30-31):

> bernoulli(stan::io::var_context& context__, std::ostream* pstream__ = 0) : prob_grad::prob_grad(0)

this supposed to be

> bernoulli(stan::io::var_context& context__, std::ostream* pstream__ = 0) : prob_grad(0)

I simply modified src/stan/gm/generator.hpp at line around 2306 from

> o << INDENT2 << ": prob_grad::prob_grad(0) {"

to

> #ifdef WIN32
>       o << INDENT2 << ": prob_grad(0) {"
> #else
>       o << INDENT2 << ": prob_grad::prob_grad(0) {"
> #endif

3. Missing dynamic or static Boost library
In visual studio, we must compile boost to compile stan program.
Also, boost1.54.0 does not compatible with visual studio 2013, so stan program does not compile in vs2013. we must use vs2012 or we must upgrade boost to 1.56 which is under development.

the last is good news. The bernoulli example ran!

I will give an instruction how to compile stan in visual studio when I have time.

messages.subject: Specifying and fitting multi-level models with group level predictors.
messages.subject_clean: Specifying and fitting multi-level models with group level predictors.
messages.body_plain:
Hello stan users,
I'm struggling to fit a multi-level model with stan. I often have problems with convergence, where each chain just runs in parallel.

I am working with soil moisture data from an observational experiment. Our experiment is set up with 8 sites in the control treatment, and 8 in the removal treatment. Each of the 16 sites contains two dataloggers, each with 4 soil moisture probes attached. We observe soil moisture at the probe level. I want to fit a model of the mean soil moisture over two days (24 hourly samples) for each probe, and the treatment effect, which is applied at the site level.

I started with the simplest model with semi-informative priors (see pre_mean_basic.stan).
moisture ~ normal(mu_control + treatment * b_trt, sigma_moisture)
This model fit efficiently after 200 iterations. However I did not estimate probe level means, just treatment effects.

To estimate probe level means I added a layer to the model (see pre_mean_ml.stan).
moisture[i] ~ normal(a_probe[probe[i]], sigma_moisture)
a_probe ~ N(mu_control + treatment * b_trt, sigma_probe)
This model does not fit efficiently, 400 iterations result in reasonable n_eff and Rhats for the probe level means, but not for the site level intercept or treatment slope. The traceplots show poor mixing.

I also tried recreating most of the experimental structure in the multi-level model by adding a site layer above the probe layer (see pre_mean_mls.stan).
moisture[i] ~ N(a_probe[probe[i]], sigma_moisture)
a_probe[j] ~ N(a_site[site[j]], sigma_probe)
a_site ~ N(mu_control + treatment * b_trt, sigma_site)
This model is slower to fit than the two-level model, but n_eff/N is higher for all parameters, and the traceplots show better convergence and mixing.

Is there a more efficient way to specify and fit these models? I'll use the best specification to repeatedly fit (secret weapon style) the model to each day in our time-series (~1000).

Since these are time-series data, observations are highly correlated within each probe. The nature of the correlation changes from day to day depending on rainfall. I'm not sure how to account for this in the model without introducing massive covariance matrices. Is there a more efficient method? I've considered fitting a gaussian process to the time-series within each probe to understand within day trends, but I'm not sure if that will help with the auto-correlation or not.

Thanks,
Joey

The basic model's just a constrained linear regression with

  real<lower=0,upper=1> mu_control;

constrained the parameters so tightly.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] How does the adaptation of the diagonal metric work?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] How does the adaptation of the diagonal metric work?
messages.body_plain:
As Bob noted the adaptation procedure is discussed in the manual.

Warmup is separated into multiple “slow” and “fast” phases.  In
a fast phases only the step size is adapted, while in the slow phases
both the step size and the metric are adapted.  More specifically,
in a slow phase the step size is dynamically optimized with dual
averaging while the sample covariance is aggregated and at the
end of the slow phase the sample covariance is used to update
the metric.

Currently warmup begins with a fast phase meant to find high
probability mass.  A series of expanding slow phases then
learn the metric before a final fast phase makes final tweaks
to the step size after the last update to the metric.

Sorry about that --- it never should've went into the doc.  There's
really not a good way to do integer floor or ceiling right now in Stan
(or round).  I just added to the next release doc issue to get rid
of that doc.  (Or we'll add the functions and update the doc.)

They have the signatures the way they do because it matches the
usage in the C++ library, but in C++ you can just assign a double
to an integer and it'll cast --- we explicitly stop users from doing
that in Stan.

So we'll need a floor and ceil function for integers,
maybe ifloor and iceil (to align with fmax and fmin and fabs).
The closest we have now is int_step, which is not very helpful
here, though could be hacked if the integers weren't too large.
There's already an issue:

https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/374

and Michael's already raised objections because it's not
theoretically kosher with HMC (though in some interpolation
cases it'd be OK, which is why it's in the doc as such).
But then the real-valued versions are just as incompatible
and we already have those.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Question about increment_log_prob()
messages.body_plain:
There's no way to speed it up because it's already optimized!

Loops are fast in Stan already, because they're just compiled to C++.

In Stan, the speed boost from vectorization comes from reducing
the size of the expression tree involved in automatic differentiation.
The increment_log_prob() function itself uses an accumulator so that
the effect of calling it multiple times stores up the value and then
produces a single node in the expression tree with all the summands
as operands.

More specifically, given an array

  real foo[N];

the Stan code

  for (n in 1:N)
    increment_log_prob(foo[n]);

is translated to C++ as:

  for (int n = 1; n <= N; ++n)
    lp_accumulator.add(foo[n-1]);

where lp_accumulator is an instance of stan::math::accumulator.

In contrast, the Stan code

  increment_log_prob(foo);

is translated to C++ as:

  lp_accumulator.add(foo);

Now the reason they are roughly the same is that the
accumulator class is defined this way:

   template <typename T>
    class accumulator {
    private:
      std::vector<T> buf_;

...
      template <typename S>
      typename boost::enable_if<boost::is_arithmetic<S>, void>::type
      add(S x) {
        buf_.push_back(static_cast<T>(x));
      }

     template <typename S>
      void add(const std::vector<S>& xs) {
        for (size_t i = 0; i < xs.size(); ++i)
          add(xs[i]);
      }
...

So it works out to almost identical C++ code.  There is a bit more indirection
in the vectorized call, but that'll almost certainly be inlined by the compiler.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Hi Bob,

On Tuesday, March 11, 2014 2:20:14 PM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>
> On Mar 11, 2014, at 4:46 PM, Joey Reid <reid...@umn.edu> wrote:
>
> > Hello stan users,
> > I'm struggling to fit a multi-level model with stan. I often have problems with convergence, where each chain just runs in parallel.
>
> Was that for  pre_mean_ml.stan?

Yes, especially for pre_mean_ml, but also for pre_mean_mls to a lessor degree.

>
> > I am working with soil moisture data from an observational experiment. Our experiment is set up with 8 sites in the control treatment, and 8 in the removal treatment. Each of the 16 sites contains two dataloggers, each with 4 soil moisture probes attached. We observe soil moisture at the probe level. I want to fit a model of the mean soil moisture over two days (24 hourly samples) for each probe, and the treatment effect, which is applied at the site level.
> >
> > I started with the simplest model with semi-informative priors (see pre_mean_basic.stan).
> > moisture ~ normal(mu_control + treatment * b_trt, sigma_moisture)
> > This model fit efficiently after 200 iterations. However I did not estimate probe level means, just treatment effects.
>
> The basic model's just a constrained linear regression with
> some fairly broad priors over the constrained range.  So that
> shouldn't be a problem, though I don't understand the motivation
> for the priors.
>
> > To estimate probe level means I added a layer to the model (see pre_mean_ml.stan).
> > moisture[i] ~ normal(a_probe[probe[i]], sigma_moisture)
> > a_probe ~ N(mu_control + treatment * b_trt, sigma_probe)
> > This model does not fit efficiently, 400 iterations result in reasonable n_eff and Rhats for the probe level means, but not for the site level intercept or treatment slope. The traceplots show poor mixing.
>
> I can imagine it would give you problems given this
> specification of mean:
>
>   mu_pre_pid <- mu_control + pidtrt * b_pre  + sigma_pre_pid * eta_pre_pid;
>
> given that these are all parameters:
>
>   real<lower=0,upper=1> mu_control;
>   real<lower=-1,upper=1> b_pre;
>   vector[Npid] eta_pre_pid;
>   real<lower=0,upper=10> sigma_pre_pid; // sd of pids
>
> and only this is data:
>
>   vector<lower=0,upper=1>[Npid] pidtrt; // links probe to treatment
>
> There is a serious additive non-identifiability due to
> mu_control and sigma_pre_pid * eta_pre_pid, as well as
> a multiplicative identifiability on sigma_pre_pid * eta_pre_pid
>
> The choice of relatively broad priors also seems odd given that you've
> constrained the parameters so tightly.
>
> - Bob
>

Thanks for that, I knew I was overlooking something important. I did two things that seem to have helped a lot. First, I changed the model specification to the standard normal(mu_control + pidtrt * b_pre, sigma_pre_pid), which allowed me to drop the eta parameters, which increased speed. I still had convergence problems, so I scaled and centered the y variable (prevwc, originally a proportion [0,1]). All of the models now converge and run much faster.

Thanks again for looking at this, it was hugely helpful.

Joey

Bob: Why in Huu's version there is softmax but in your posting the quotation of Huu's code has log_softmax? Did you edit that?

Huu's new code is still impractically slow with n=40.

The n_eff depends very much on much "jitter" is added to the diagonal
 > if_else(i==j, 0.0001, 0.0)
as larger jitter makes the latent function less constrained by softmax.  The Markov chain is run in n-dimensional space (ignoring now the covariance function parameters), but the latent function is constrained in n-1 dimensional manifold. Jitter allows the Markov chain to move a little bit away from the manifold. Iideally the amount of jitter should be zero, but for example, if the jitter is set to 0.0000001, n_eff is approximately 20 with n=4000.

In autumn Michael said that had obtained huge speed-up by using simplex in some of his models and if I remember correctly the reason would be because then the chain is also in n-1 dimensional space.

I could not figure out how to use simplex with Cholesky version, as now alpha~normal(0,1) is the sampled parameter...

Aki

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Logistic GP
messages.body_plain:
Aki,

Let me be a little more detailed about the importance of the simplex.  We do indeed have a Markov chain sampling from an n-dimensional space but the important part is that the latent function, and hence the data, are only sensitive
to an (n - 1) dimensional submanifold.  That means that directions transverse to that submanifold are unconstrained, and the chain will just drift around in a random walk.  The simplex allows us to enforce the constraint analytically
so we can sample from the (n - 1) dimensional space and avoid the performance-reducing drift.

That said we have to be really careful here.  Firstly, the simplex parameters are already defined to be positive -- recall that a simplex is a collection { p_i } satisfying p_i > 0 and sum_i p_i = 1 -- so the f = log℗ is actually making your
posterior worse.  Moreover, the GP shouldn't be in the n dimensional observation space but rather the (n - 1) dimensional latent space.  So what you want is something like

f ~ GP( mean, covariance function)
p ~ simplex_map(f)
y ~ binomial℗

where simplex_map is a map from the latent space to the observation space, R^{n - 1} -> R^{n}.  Unfortunately this isn't exposed and I'm not sure if there's an easy way to do this right now in Stan. Let me start a separate thread
for that.

-Mike

On Mar 14, 2014, at 12:19 PM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Aki,
>
> Let me be a little more detailed about the importance of the simplex.  We do indeed have a Markov chain sampling from an n-dimensional space but the important part is that the latent function, and hence the data, are only sensitive
> to an (n - 1) dimensional submanifold.  That means that directions transverse to that submanifold are unconstrained, and the chain will just drift around in a random walk.  The simplex allows us to enforce the constraint analytically
> so we can sample from the (n - 1) dimensional space and avoid the performance-reducing drift.
>
> That said we have to be really careful here.  Firstly, the simplex parameters are already defined to be positive -- recall that a simplex is a collection { p_i } satisfying p_i > 0 and sum_i p_i = 1 -- so the f = log℗ is actually making your
> posterior worse.  Moreover, the GP shouldn't be in the n dimensional observation space but rather the (n - 1) dimensional latent space.  So what you want is something like
>
> f ~ GP( mean, covariance function)
> p ~ simplex_map(f)
> y ~ binomial℗

If p is a simplex, then you probably want a multinomial or
categorical for y.

>
> where simplex_map is a map from the latent space to the observation space, R^{n - 1} -> R^{n}.  Unfortunately this isn't exposed and I'm not sure if there's an easy way to do this right now in Stan. Let me start a separate thread
> for that.

The problem is that our softmax() is defined on R^n -> R^n, so it takes
a redundant parameterization for the input.  Now what you can do is use
a point in R^(n-1) and set one of the values to 0.

But we should really have a softmaxKminus1() function or something like that
that works on R^(n-1) -> R^n.   And perhaps the inverse_softmaxKminus1() that
goes the other way around.

This is all related to the discussions we had with Andrew about whether to
use K or (K-1) dimensions.  I believe the issue with using (K-1) is that
the prior becomes asymmetric.  I seem to recall that Andrew preferred the
K-ary version, which is why it's the way it is.  In retrospect, I think we
should've done it the other way around.  We can just let users do it either
way using a new softmax function defined on (n-1).

If you do it with K parameters, you need stronger priors to keep the estimates
well-behaved so they don't just drift around as Michael points out they will do.

- Bob

Thanks

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] bivariate normal-gamma distribution in stan
messages.body_plain:
Hi Bob,

   I have attached a simplest stan-code (alpha = 1.1 and beta = 0.5).

According to Wikipedia (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Normal-gamma_distribution),  an analytic mean, mode and variance are given by

x:
  Mean:x
  Mode:x
  StdDev:sqrt(beta/(lambda*(alpha-1)))
tau:
  Mean:alpha/beta
  Mode:(alpha-0.5)/beta
  StdDev:sqrt(alpha/beta^2)

Case 1: mu = -4.3, alpha = 1.1, beta = 0.5
Expected Values:
x:
  Mean:-4.3
  Mode:-4.3
  StdDev:sqrt(50/31) ~ 1.270...
tau:
  Mean:2.2
  Mode:1.2
  Variance:4.4

Case 1 Results:
x:
  Mean: -4.301 (OK)
  Mode:-4.300 (OK)
  StdDev:1.033 (slightly off due to tau)
tau:
  Mean: 2.246 (2% off. considering MCSE = 5.262e-3, this error is a bit large)
  Mode: 1.200 (Exact)
  StdDev:2.133 (off a half an expected value)

Case 2:mu = -4.3, alpha = 9.0, beta = 4.0 (the code is not attached.)
Expected Values:
x:
  Mean:-4.3
  Mode:-4.3
  StdDev:sqrt(155)/31 ~ 0.401609
tau:
  Mean:2.25
  Mode:2.125
  StdDev:0.5625

Case 2 Results:
x:
  Mean:-4.300 (OK)
  Mode:-4.300 (OK)
  StdDev:0.3991 (close enough)
tau:
  Mean:2.251 (close enough)
  Mode:2.125 (OK)
  StdDev:0.7438 (a bit off)

To reproduce the results, I used the following arguments:

./normal-gamma-version1.exe sample num_warmup=10000 num_samples=1000000 random seed=324393 init=normal-gamma-version1.init.R

As a note, a gamma distribution with alpha = 1.1 and beta = 0.5 is a heavy-tale distribution (this could be a reason). 2% error seems to be small, but the normal-gamma is a conjugate prior to the lognormal distribution and 2% error is deadly significant to my case...

Thank you for your help and kindness.

Shota

messages.subject: return to lmer vs stan
messages.body_plain:
I am dipping my toes into stan, coming from a background in maximum likelihood estimation of linear mixed-effects models (I am one of the authors of the lme4 package for R and also of the MixedModels package for Julia). I also have some familiarity with C++, Rcpp and Eigen having done the interface between R/Rcpp and Eigen for the RcppEigen package.

I have at least skimmed the Reference Manual for Stan 2.2.0 and read some of the sections pretty thoroughly.

I very much like the idea of the

cholesky_factor_cov

and

cholesky_factor_cor

classes.  As the Stan authors may know, lmer uses the elements of the cholesky_factor_cov representation of the (relative) covariance matrices for the random effects as the parameters being directly optimized in the maximum likelihood estimation of parameters.  (The fixed-effects coefficients and the residual standard deviation are profiled out of the log-likelihood function.)

My first question is regarding a prior on the parameters in a cholesky_factor_cor object.  Sections 46 and 47 of the manual discuss distributions of covariance matrices and correlation matrices.  Is it possible to assign a prior distribution to the Cholesky factor directly? For example, in the lkj_corr_log method defined in lkj_corr.hpp the correlation matrix is factored before being passed to lkj_corr_choleksy, but lkj_corr_cholesky_log.  Have I missed a definition of lkj_corr_cholesky or lkj_cov_cholesky to be used in an expression like

L~lkj_corr_cholesky(eta)

or do I go the direct route and call lkj_corr_cholesky_log to increment the log probability?

messages.subject_clean: collapsing model matrices to unique rows
messages.body_plain:

However, in the model matrix for the fixed-effects parameters there are only 4 distinct rows.  For the random effects there are 244 distinct combinations of id, c1, c2 and c3.

It occurs to me that there may be considerable savings in collapsing information in the model matrices to the unique rows and having an index vector to associate the rows of the collapsed model matrix with the observations.  It is not difficult to do the collasping in R

> mm <- model.matrix(rt ~ c1 + c2 + c3, dat)
> str(mm)

 - attr(*, "dimnames")=List of 2
  ..$ : chr [1:28710] "1" "2" "3" "5" ...
  ..$ : chr [1:4] "(Intercept)" "c1" "c2" "c3"
 - attr(*, "assign")= int [1:4] 0 1 2 3
> unique(mm)
    (Intercept)    c1   c2    c3
1             1  0.25  0.5 -0.75
49            1  0.25  0.5  0.25
97            1  0.25 -0.5  0.25
145           1 -0.75 -0.5  0.25

(creating the index vector may be a bit clumsier but not too formidable).

In a Stan model the vector of coefficients could be pre-multiplied by this 4 by 4 matrix producing a 4-vector of unique contributions then the model for rt[n] would have a contribution of fixef[ind[n]] to the mean.

The reason I think this could help is because evaluating the gradient of an indexing operation would, I believe, be faster than evaluating the gradient of a multiplication by a model matrix with nearly 29000 rows.

Does this seem worthwhile exploring, keeping in mind that I am still at the "See Dick sample" stage of writing Stan models.

messages.body_plain:
On Mar 17, 2014, at 6:32 PM, Douglas Bates <dmb...@gmail.com> wrote:

> I am dipping my toes into stan,

Welcome!

> coming from a background in maximum likelihood estimation of linear mixed-effects models (I am one of the authors of the lme4 package for R and also of the MixedModels package for Julia).

We've all heard a lot about lme4 from Andrew (who calls it "lmer").
We've been spending some time going the other way and thinking
about (penalized) MLE and (penalized) maximum marginal likelihood for
Stan.

> I also have some familiarity with C++, Rcpp and Eigen having done the interface between R/Rcpp and Eigen for the RcppEigen package.
>
> I have at least skimmed the Reference Manual for Stan 2.2.0 and read some of the sections pretty thoroughly.
>
> I very much like the idea of the
>
> cholesky_factor_cov
>
> and
>
> cholesky_factor_cor
>
> classes.  As the Stan authors may know, lmer uses the elements of the cholesky_factor_cov representation of the (relative) covariance matrices for the random effects as the parameters being directly optimized in the maximum likelihood estimation of parameters.  (The fixed-effects coefficients and the residual standard deviation are profiled out of the log-likelihood function.)

Only a few of us are versed in the lme4 code.

> My first question is regarding a prior on the parameters in a cholesky_factor_cor object.  Sections 46 and 47 of the manual discuss distributions of covariance matrices and correlation matrices.  Is it possible to assign a prior distribution to the Cholesky factor directly? For example, in the lkj_corr_log method defined in lkj_corr.hpp the correlation matrix is factored before being passed to lkj_corr_choleksy, but lkj_corr_cholesky_log.  Have I missed a definition of lkj_corr_cholesky or lkj_cov_cholesky to be used in an expression like
>
> L~lkj_corr_cholesky(eta)
>
> or do I go the direct route and call lkj_corr_cholesky_log to increment the log probability?

That function no longer exists as of Stan 2.2 (though it's still there in C++ if
that's what you're after).  We're going to bring it back when we've added the cholesky_corr data type,
which is nearly ready to go.  Without the data type, the density's useless because you'd have to
do the decomposition and Jacobian adjustment yourself in the Stan code, which
is pretty awful.

For now (Stan 2.2), you have to go the roundabout way of defining
a correlation matrix parameter:

parameters {
  ...
  corr_matrix[K] Omega;
  ...
}

and then give it an LKJ prior:

model {
  matrix[K,K] L;   // local variable

  Omega ~ lkj_corr(nu);  // prior directly on correlation matrix
  L <- cholesky_decompose(Omega);

  ... use L ...
}

This introduces a lot of redundant calculations because the underlying representation
for Omega in the unconstrained space is as its Cholesky factor, so we have to
do a redundant multiplication and Jacobian adjustment to get to the correlation
matrix itself in the constrained space, and then I believe lkj_corr does the Cholesky
factorization under the hood, and then cholesky_decompose does the factorization again.

All the redundant calculation will go away when we have the cholesky_corr data type, and
you'll be able to write something like this (we'll probably simplify the name of the
density):

parameters {
  cholesky_corr L;
  ...
model {
  L ~ lkj_cholesky(nu);
  ... use L ...

Ben Goodrich has a neat paper comparing Wishart and LKJ-style priors (he was
the one driving the design of these parts of the code):

  http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/research/unpublished/Visualization.pdf

We're also adding a quad_form_diag(Omega,sigma) function in the next release
of Stan that will do

  diag_matrix(sigma) * Omega * diag_matrix(sigma)

to make the kind of scaled covariance priors Andrew and Ben like easier to express.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] return to lmer vs stan
messages.body_plain:
Hi Doug,

Good to hear from you again. As Bob mentioned, the lkj_corr_cholesky() function is easier to use incorrectly than to use correctly, which is why it is slated to get disappeared for a while. In short, I intended it to be an internal-only C++ function but it accidentally got exposed to the Stan language in the initial release of Stan. The only reason to use it that is still valid (i.e. it corresponds to the posterior distribution you defined) is if a correlation matrix is a parameter and you need its Cholesky factor for some subsequent calculation. In that case,

model {
  L <- cholesky_decompose(correlation_matrix);
  L ~ lkj_choleksy_corr(eta); // this confusingly implies correlation_matrix ~ lkj_corr(eta)
  // use L in a subsequent calculation to avoid recalculating it
}

In all other cases in the Stan language,

foo ~ some_distribution();

means that you are putting a prior on foo itself.

What, you, I, and everybody else really needs is for the Cholesky factor of a correlation matrix to be a primitive type in Stan. This is possible with some convoluted hand-written Stan code that I am attaching. It constructs L via something equivalent to the onion method described in the LKJ (2008) paper such that

L * L' ~ lkj_corr(eta);

without actually forming that matrix product. To verify (a necessary condition that) L * L' has the LKJ distribution, you can do in R

library(rstan)
K <- 11
posterior <- stan(file = "onion.stan", data = list(K = K, eta = 1))
correlation_matrices <- extract(posterior, "Sigma")[[1]]
rho <- correlation_matrices[,1,2]
qqplot(rho, -1 + 2 * rbeta(length(rho), K / 2, K / 2), pch = 20)
abline(a = 0, b = 1, col = "red", lty = "dashed")

Hope that helps,
Ben
