messages.body_plain:
I am trying to develop a zero / one inflated beta regression model using rstan.  The idea is that 0s and 1s are modeled using a bernoulli distribution, (0,1) are modeled using a beta distribution. I have attached the R code and the Stan model code.

The gamlss.dist <http://www.google.com/url?sa=t&rct=j&q=&esrc=s&source=web&cd=2&ved=0CDMQFjAB&url=http%3A%2F%2Fcran.at.r-project.org%2Fweb%2Fpackages%2Fgamlss.dist%2Fgamlss.dist.pdf&ei=C0cnU5i7N6GZ0AHNi4GABQ&usg=AFQjCNHv0uGmqB9vC9GYdfVZit8Wo2MRFw&sig2=7R-cHqKitF0l7eBj_V9MNA&bvm=bv.62922401,d.dmQ> package has a beta inflated distribution, BEINF. The R code uses that to generate example data.  The R code also uses the gamlss function to compare against the stan model.

There are four parameters for the model: mu, lambda, nu, tau.  Mu is the mean of the beta distribution, lambda is the total count.  I am following the re-parameterization of Beta from the Stan Reference 2.2.0 p. 155.  Nu is the probability of getting 0 / probability of (0,1).  Tau is the probability of getting 0 / probability (0,1).  Each parameter is modeled using an intercept and coefficients, with normal distribution for the priors.

The main problem is this: the model does a particularly poor job of estimating the lambda intercept, and sometimes the lambda coefficients.  (It does fine with everything else).  Using 4 chains, this is how it compares:
lambda_intercept
actual: 1, model: 2.3 (2.0–2.6)

lambda_coef1
actual: 0.2, model: 0.5 (0.2–0.6)

lambda_coef2
actual: -0.5, model: -0.5 (-0.7 – -0.5)

Is this variation to be expected or am I doing something wrong?  I am getting a few of these messages:
Informational Message: The current Metropolis proposal is about to be rejected becuase of the following issue:
Error in function stan::prob::bernoulli_log(N4stan5agrad3varE): Probability parameter is -nan:0, but must be finite!

Informational Message: The current Metropolis proposal is about to be rejected becuase of the following issue:
Error in function stan::prob::beta_log(N4stan5agrad3varE): Second shape parameter is 0:0, but must be > 0!

I imagine that there is a lot I could do to improve on this model.  Any help is appreciated!  Thanks!

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] ZeroOne Inflated Beta Regression
messages.body_plain:
The mixture model you wrote for 0/1 inflation is here:

  if (y[n] == 0)
    increment_log_prob(bernoulli_log(1, p0));
  else if (y[n] == 1)
    increment_log_prob(bernoulli_log(1, p1));
  else
    increment_log_prob(beta_log(y[n], alpha, beta) + bernoulli_log(1, p2));

I find this a very confusing way to write a mixture of a bernoulli
and beta, when you could just write it out more directly using
phi as the mixing ratio as

  if (y[n] == 0 || y[n] == 1)
    increment_log_prob(bernoulli_log(y[n] | p) + bernoulli_log(1,phi))
  else
    increment_log_prob(beta_log(y[n], alpha, beta) + bernoulli_log(0,phi));

I think we should add (real / vector);  a better hack for real x divided
by vector v is:

 rep_vector(x,size(v)) ./ v

To answer your question, the amount of variation from the expected values
depend both on the amount of data and whether the model you wrote down
actually identifies the parameters.  I'd worry about there being too
many degrees of freedom in your encoding with both tau and nu.

But as always, I'd suggest working up from a simple model.  In this case
it might be one where there's only an intercept, say, or not even a regression,
just a simple mixture estimating alpha, beta and phi above.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
To illustrate what I mean, consider just a linear regression model for the example I mentioned.  The full model matrix is 28710 by 4 but there are only 4 distinct rows.  I wasn't trying to pool the data, just replace large matrix multiplications by a much smaller matrix multiplication followed by indexing operations.  My model specification with the small matrix multiplication is

data {
    int<lower=0>             N; // number of observations
    int<lower=0>             P; // number of regression coefficients
    matrix[C,P]       cntrasts; // contrast matrix
    vector[N]               rt; // response
    matrix[N,P]             mm; // full model matrix
    int<lower=1,upper=C> tr[N]; // indices of factor tar
}
parameters {
    real<lower=0>      sigma_y;
    vector[P]             beta; // Fixed-effects coefficients
}
model {
    vector[N]          linpred; // conditional mean of the responses
    vector[C]         cntrbeta;

    beta ~ normal(0, 10);       // diffuse prior on components of beta
    sigma_y ~ cauchy(0,4);
    cntrbeta <- cntrasts * beta;
    for (n in 1:N)
        linpred[n] <- cntrbeta[tr[n]];
//    linpred <- mm * beta;
    rt ~ normal(linpred, sigma_y);
}

The mm, cntrasts and tr matrices and vectors are such that

all.equal(mm, cntrasts[tr,])

is TRUE in R.

messages.body_plain:
There are two major ways the negative binomial is defined in the literature. One is the way followed by R, DeGroot, Wolfram, etc. and the other is the way followed by Gelman, Wikipedia, etc. Stan is following the Gelman parametrization (which makes sense as Dr. Gelman is one of the key people behind Stan) so (unless I made an error with the algebra) neg_binomial(alpha, beta) represents a distribution with mean (alpha / beta) and variance alpha * (1 + beta) / beta^2.

Does that help?

> But as you write an " \alpha -1" in the definition of the density function, should I write: "Count[i] ~ NegBin( N[i]+1, 1/mu)"?

Stan uses the parametrization of Bayesian Data Analysis book, comparing to wikipedia's definition you'll have (1-p)=beta/(beta+1) and r=alpha.

Is N[i] the number of failures until the experiment is stopped? Or is it the number of successes until the experiment is stopped. Both parametrizations ocorr in literature.

If it's the latter, then
Count[i] ~ NegBin( N[i], 1/f)  in your parametrization is
Count[i] ~ neg_binomial( N[i], f-1) in Stan parametrization

If it's the former, then
Count[i] ~ NegBin( N[i], 1/f)  in your parametrization is
Count[i] ~ neg_binomial( N[i], 1/(f-1)) in Stan parametrization

Note: this wasn't tested, so confirm that this calculations are correct in simple example before using them

Thanks for the working example!

I just realized you'd need the responses to match as well in order to pool
the data, so that's not going to work in general.

But you could pool the predictors in the call to normal().
Supposing that the elements of rt are sorted by condition and
count[c] is the number of elements with condition c, then you could have:

{
  int start;
  start <- 1;
  for (c in 1:C) {
    segment(rt, start, count[c]) ~ normal(cntrbeta[c], sigma_y);
    start <- start + count[c];
  }
}

The segment(v,i,n) function returns a vector with elements v[i], ..., v[i + n - 1].

It's ugly, but you could build an appropriate copy of rt in Stan's
transformed data block, which is only executed once on data read.'

I'm not sure there'd another factor of 3 in speedup, though it would
be considerably tighter in memory given the way our expression trees
are built up.

This is the kind of thing where it'd be nice to have a ragged array
data structure.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
All,

I am working on a project where I have 5 correlated outcomes observed for units ( 5 organs), clustered inside of individuals. Sample size (number of  individuals) is very small N=4-6, depending on context.

I have several covariates (N=19) with which to predict outcomes, that are unique at the individual level. Outcomes vary in terms of their support. Some outcomes are Gaussian, some are binary categories.

So in total we have 5 outcome measures for  5 "organs", clustered into 5 individuals, and 19 covariates with measures unique only at the individual level (the highest level in this hierarchy).

Thus the basic model setup is as below in pseudo-code (note my poor use of  the letter l, which looks like the number 1):
G[l,n]~Normal(b[l,1] + b[l,2]*X[n], sdG)

H[l,n]~Normal(b[l,3] + b[l,4]*X[n], sdH)

Y[l,n]~Bernouli(inv_logit(b[l,3] + b[l,4]*X[n]))
...

Where:

b[l,1:N]~mvn(mu[1:N],Sigma[1:N,1:N])

all of the cholesky parametrization is done to optimize, and proper priors get declared, etc...

The above model works fine, and I can use WAIC to compare each predictor, by comparing each of the 19 bivariate models, and a null intercept only model.

I was recently pointed to Bayesian lasso procedures as an alternate analytic strategy where (in pseudo-stan code):
G[l,n]~Normal(X[n]*b[l,1:19], sdG)

H[l,n]~Normal(X[n]*b[l,20:38], sdH)

Y[l,n]~Bernouli(inv_logit(X[n]*b[l,39:50something]))
...

Where:
b[l]~mvn(mu,Sigma)

and mu has sharply regularizing double_exponential priors

This model wont run because Sigma is a large 95X95 matrix. The problem persists even
where:
Sigma <- diag_matrix(sigma) * cholesky_decompose(Rho);

In fact it is this line of code that throws the error:
  (Warmup)Error : error in call to cholesky decomposition; require symmetric matrix, but found; x[9,32]=0.0088246; x[32,9]=0.0088246

Since sample size is so small, and the outcomes variables are highly correlated measures of essentially the same empirical outcome,  I really like the idea of letting the regression parameters be drawn from a multivariate normal, rather than assuming that they are independent things.

Is it possible to get something like this running in Stan? I have seen threads on here about hand coding a hack to get around the computational burdens of such a big cov matrix, but they were used when the matrix was known data. Is there any similar strategies when the matrix is random?

Sigma is a correlation matrix, and thus has a Cholesky factor. But rather than declaring Sigma in the parameters block and subsequently calculating its Cholesky factorization (which is slow and prone to numerical errors that you ran into when the dimension is large), it is much better to declare the ingredients of its Cholesky factor in the parameters block, construct and use the Cholesky factor, and never actually form Sigma (unless you want to). Also, this can be combined with a multivariate Matt trick to avoid calling any of the multi_normal() functions.

Maybe the new attachment is clearer. Basically, you do a lot of convoluted stuff to construct L such that L * L' is a correlation matrix with an LKJ distribution. Then, you use the fact that if

b[l] <- mu + sigma .* (L * z[l]);

messages.subject_clean: decomposing additive kernel functions in GP
messages.body_plain:
Hi -

I'm currently working on a GP-based poisson regression time-series model with a smooth component modeling a long-term trend (following a squared exponential kernel, k_s(x,x')) and a periodic component representing seasonality in disease incidence, i.e. k_p(x,x') = exp(-nu*sin^2(pi*(x-x'))), where nu is the frequency of the periodic component. So the covariance between two points is defined by k(x,x') = k_s(x,x') + k_p(x,x'). The data are reported as weekly counts over the course of about 7 years, and I assume that the periodic component has frequency 1/52.

This model is similar in spirit to the one that showed up on Andrew's blog for the birthday data a couple of years ago:

http://andrewgelman.com/2012/06/19/slick-time-series-decomposition-of-the-birthdays-data/

I'm wondering what the best way would be to then take a look at the rate ratios for each component, i.e. the long-term trend versus the seasonal components, as in the plots of the day of year, day of week, etc contributions in the birthday data blog post.

Currently, for the seasonal component I'm planning on simulating from the GP posterior with the week of the year varying (i.e. from 1 to 52) and holding fixed the total number of weeks in the data, i.e. at 1. Would this be likely to yield the quantities I'm looking for?

The other idea I had was to just break them apart into separate vars in the estimation, each with their own covariance, and then bring them back together  when evaluating the data likelihood, i.e. y_log_seasonal[t] + y_log_trend[t], but I was hoping to avoid doing this to keep the computational overhead down, and also wasn't sure if this would be equivalent to bringing them together in the covariance matrix.

Any ideas or suggestions would be greatly appreciated!

-Jon

messages.subject: Re: decomposing additive kernel functions in GP
messages.subject_clean: decomposing additive kernel functions in GP
messages.body_plain:
If f=f_1+f_2 and f_1~GP(mu_1,C_1), f_2~GP(mu_2,C_2) then f~GP(mu_1+mu_2,C_1+C2), so you can break them apart into separate vars.

For the composition, first consider Gaussian case with
 y=f_1+f_2+e, where e~N(0,sigma^2)

When you want to look at the f_1 you can write
 y=f_1+e', where e'~N(mu_2+0,C_2+sigma^2)
and now you have divided the model to interesting signal f_1 and uninteresting correlated noise e'. Then you just use the usual prediction equations.

Correspondingly when you want to look at the f_2 you can write
 y=f_2+e', where e'~N(mu_1+0,C_1+sigma^2)
and now f_2 is the interesting signal.

For non-Gaussian models you just focus on the latent function
 f=f_1+f_2
but the conditioning that which part is signal and which is noise is handled in the same way.

I also recommend using product of periodic and squared exponential, so that the shape of the periodic component can change in time. This was used in birthdays example,see e.g how weekday effect changes in time.

I predict that in the future Stan will have better support for GPs, but meantime if you can install Octave, you might try GPstuff-toolbox, as it has all these implemented and much faster inference :)

Aki

messages.subject: Speed/parameter estimation in hierarchical logistic regression
messages.subject_clean: Speed/parameter estimation in hierarchical logistic regression
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I'm a newcomer to both R and stan, so apologies if this question seems trivial - I couldn't find a similar thread on the message board yet.

BACKGROUND: I've turned to Rstan to analyse a large psychology study that we've run. We have several thousand subjects in the study. Each subject is making a series of 22 binary responses in a decision-making task, with several different variables that can influence each decision. My aim is to characterise the influence of each of these variables on subjects' choices, but also to study how this varies across the population.

The way I would traditionally have done this would just be to run logistic regression on each subject's responses individually, and then fit a second model to characterise variation in these models' parameter estimates across the population. However, because there are only 22 observations per subject with several variables, this approach runs into problems of perfect separation in some subjects, and so it seems sensible to me to approach this with a hierarchical logistic model (something I haven't done before).

PROBLEM: I am starting out by trying this on data simulated in MATLAB, to ensure fitting the model returns sensible values. To keep things simple, I've limited myself to 50 subjects. There are three parameters to be estimated for each subject, drawn from a normal distribution across the population. Each subject's true parameters are drawn from a normal distribution, with non-zero mean and std. of 3.

For me, the main goal of the exercise is to reliably recover the non-zero means for each parameter, and reliably estimate the population std. to be 3. This works just fine for hierarchical linear regression (that is, if I simulate linear observations rather than binary responses) - Rstan runs fast, and correctly returns the underlying population means and stds. of the parameter estimates. But for hierarchical logistic, it (a) takes a long time to estimate - 10 minutes as opposed to a few seconds, and this scales with the number of subjects, and (b) typically squashes the estimated population std. to 0 for each parameter, meaning that I don't get any estimate of population variability.

Might anyone be able to provide some advice on whether the problems I'm having are because I've mis-specified my model, or are because the problem is ill-posed in some way?

Many thanks,
Laurence

p.s. R, stan, matlab code and example data are attached. The R.matlab library has to be installed to run the readMat command in the r script.

messages.subject: Rescaling
messages.body_plain:
In order to identify an IRT model I’m working on, I’m experimenting with the scaling and normalizing approach from ARM (and cribbing from https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/blob/feature/ARM/src/models/ARM/Ch.19/item_response.stan)

I note that there’s a typo in that example (and the book!), in that scale and shift are defined in terms of ‘a', not ‘a_raw'. The model won’t even compile in Stan as written.  OTOH, being able to rescale a parameter would address my questions below (e.g., by simply declaring a ~ normal(mu_a,sigma_a); a <- (a-mean(a))/sd(a);)

More importantly, it runs fairly slowly and returns samples for all the intermediate parameters, parameters that AFAIK can’t really be interpreted meaningfully. a_raw, b_raw, and g_raw don’t matter, except for computational convenience; we only really need a, b, and g. But sampling them and reporting them chews up memory and CPU (as I understand how Stan works). Is there a way to prevent those intermediate variables from being reported back to R, and to optimize how they’re handled internally? Ideally, they’d be local variables in the model, but I don’t think there’s a way to refactor the model to make that happen.

Indeed, I wonder if the redundant parameterization trick is as powerful in Stan as it would be in BUGS. As I understand it, that approach helps in BUGS because each parameter is updated separately, while they’re all updated at once in Stan, so the sort of drift described in ARM chapter 19 can’t happen, and redundant parameterization shouldn’t speed things up (in which case I’d do just as well at identifying the model by constraining various priors).

Am I understanding the various issues involved clearly, or have I failed to grok some essential truth about Stan?

> In order to identify an IRT model I'm working on, I'm experimenting with the scaling and normalizing approach from ARM (and cribbing from https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/blob/feature/ARM/src/models/ARM/Ch.19/item_response.stan)
>
> I note that there's a typo in that example (and the book!), in that scale and shift are defined in terms of 'a', not 'a_raw'. The model won't even compile in Stan as written.

Is there a model we've used as an example somewhere that doesn't compile?  If
so, we need to fix it.  the item-response example linked above compiles OK.

> OTOH, being able to rescale a parameter would address my questions below
> (e.g., by simply declaring a ~ normal(mu_a,sigma_a); a <- (a-mean(a))/sd(a);)

I'm not sure what you mean here in terms of execution order.  If you want to redefine
a in the model, it needs to be a local variable.

If you transform a first and then put it on the left of a sampling statement,
you need to account for the Jacobian of the transform.

What you could do is use the unit_vector[K] type, which constrains the
elements in the vector to have mean 0 and variance 1, and takes care of
the Jacobian internally.

> More importantly, it runs fairly slowly and returns samples for all the intermediate parameters, parameters that AFAIK can't really be interpreted meaningfully.  a_raw, b_raw, and g_raw don't matter, except for computational convenience;

The raw forms are what the HMC sampler is actually sampling,
after transforms that unconstrain all variables.  So in terms of
diagnosing issues with the sampler itself, they're what you need
to focus on.  They're also what you need to watch to monitor convergence
and mixing.

> we only really need a, b, and g.

Right --- that's what you're going to use for inference.

> But sampling them and reporting them chews up memory and CPU (as I understand how Stan works).

Not CPU so much.  The raw parameters are what's being sampled and
the transforms have to be done to expose the parameters in the model.
So there's no overhead.  It does chew up memory in RStan if you're
saving a large number of samples.  (8 bytes per parameter per sampling
iteration.)  It doesn't chew up memory in CmdStan, because it streams, but
will chew up memory in posterior diagnostics from bin/print.

> Is there a way to prevent those intermediate variables from being reported back to R, and to optimize how they're handled internally?

The only internal optimization is that they don't get printed.
All the computations have to happen in terms of the declared
parameters for sampling and conversion for use in the model.

But I think there's a way in RStan to limit the parameters that
are reported.  Look at the pars value in stan() --- you can use
it to list the parameters you want to save.

We'd recommend monitoring all the parameters (default without a pars
value) until you're sure the model's well-behaved in terms of convergence.

> Ideally, they'd be local variables in the model, but I don't think there's a way to refactor the model to make that happen.

No, you can't do that refactoring in the model unless you
can analytically marginalize a parameter out.

Whenever you can do that, it's a very good idea for computation.
Even if you can sample the parameter, it's almost always more efficient
in terms of inference to use an analytical marginalization.

> Indeed, I wonder if the redundant parameterization trick is as powerful in Stan as it would be in BUGS. As I understand it, that approach helps in BUGS because each parameter is updated separately, while they're all updated at once in Stan, so the sort of drift described in ARM chapter 19 can't happen, and redundant parameterization shouldn't speed things up (in which case I'd do just as well at identifying the model by constraining various priors).
>
> Am I understanding the various issues involved clearly, or have I failed to grok some essential truth about Stan?

I'll let you decide that!  The thing to read is chapter 21 of
the manual, chapter "Execution of a Stan Program".  It goes
through all the data moves and transforms and I/O.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
I am trying to analyze the ages of a bunch of zircon crystals using a Gaussian mixture model with an unspecified number of components (my gut-feeling prior is around 3 or so). I have several sets of about 100 age measurements and I want to analyze each set.

The problem is almost identical to the galaxy and acidity examples in section 22.4 of BDA (3rd ed.), or exercise 2(d) for chapter 22: I have a one-dimensional vector of about age measurements ranging from 40 to 300 kiloyears (apart from age, there is nothing to distinguish one zircon from another for the purposes of this analysis) and I want to identify clusters to help some geologist colleagues unscramble a puzzle about magma dynamics. The data isn't clearly multimodal, but it has hints of being bimodal (although that could also be noise), as well as being highly skewed with a long tail.

I can analyze the data using the EM algorithm with Fraley and Raferty's mclust R package, but I'm interested in comparing that approach to MCMC (following the discussion on pp. 523-4 of BDA and at the beginning of 22.4) and I am trying to figure out whether it's better to try this in JAGS or Stan.

So I'm wondering whether anyone has implemented anything like the galaxy and acidity examples in Stan so I can adapt them to my problem. (Of course, maybe Stan isn't the right tool for the job, since there are discrete Dirichlet-distributed parameters pi_h in the way Gelman et al. formulate the problem in 22.4, in which case a Gibbs sampler, such as JAGS, might be the better choice.)

If I can model this with Stan, I will be happy to post the model and example data, both to help others and to benefit from the wisdom of comments from folks here, who know lots more than I do.

On Mar 23, 2014, at 7:42 PM, Jonathan Gilligan <jonathan...@gmail.com> wrote:

> I am trying to analyze the ages of a bunch of zircon crystals using a Gaussian mixture model with an unspecified number of components (my gut-feeling prior is around 3 or so). I have several sets of about 100 age measurements and I want to analyze each set.
>
> The problem is almost identical to the galaxy and acidity examples in section 22.4 of BDA (3rd ed.), or exercise 2(d) for chapter 22: I have a one-dimensional vector of about age measurements ranging from 40 to 300 kiloyears (apart from age, there is nothing to distinguish one zircon from another for the purposes of this analysis) and I want to identify clusters to help some geologist colleagues unscramble a puzzle about magma dynamics. The data isn't clearly multimodal, but it has hints of being bimodal (although that could also be noise), as well as being highly skewed with a long tail.
>
> I can analyze the data using the EM algorithm with Fraley and Raferty's mclust R package, but I'm interested in comparing that approach to MCMC (following the discussion on pp. 523-4 of BDA and at the beginning of 22.4) and I am trying to figure out whether it's better to try this in JAGS or Stan.

This is the kind of problem that Stan's good at.

It's a bit trickier to model because you have to marginalize out the
discrete cluster "responsibility" parameter.  The upside is that you
get faster mixing in the sampler without the discrete parameter.

If you do comparisons with JAGS or any other software, we'd love to hear about
them.

>
> So I'm wondering whether anyone has implemented anything like the galaxy and acidity examples in Stan so I can adapt them to my problem.

Chapter 13 of the Stan manual explains mixture modeling with examples
you could follow to do this.

There are also examples of how to formulate K-means clustering as
a Gaussian mixture.

You have a wide range of choices on the prior and how the clusters
are modeled (fixed covariance matrix or estimated).

If your data are just one-dimensional (really just ages and no
other predictors?) then the model's particularly simple as you can
do it all with regular normals rather than multivariate ones.

> (Of course, maybe Stan isn't the right tool for the job, since there are discrete Dirichlet-distributed parameters pi_h in the way Gelman et al. formulate the problem in 22.4, in which case a Gibbs sampler, such as JAGS, might be the better choice.)

pi ~ dirichlet(ones);

is no problem in Stan.  You declare pi as a simplex and ones as a
vector of 1.  In fact, this is basically a no-op in Stan because
dirichlet(1...1) is the identity and that's the default prior if
one isn't specified.

It's the discrete parameters that you sample

   z[i] ~ discrete(pi);

that need to be marginalized out.

The Stan code essentially directly codes the initial mixture-model
formula (22.1) without creating an intermediate discrete parameter.

>
> If I can model this with Stan, I will be happy to post the model and example data, both to help others and to benefit from the wisdom of comments from folks here, who know lots more than I do.

Thanks.  We always like seeing concrete models.

- Bob

messages.subject: Mixture modelling and multiple modes.
messages.body_plain:
Hi,
I have attempted to implement (in Rstan) the model discussed in chapter 13 of the Stan manual v2.2.

library(rstan)
lpmodel <- '
  data {
    int<lower=1> K; // number of mixture components
    int<lower=1> N; // number of data points
    real y[N];      // observations
  }
  parameters {
    simplex[K] theta; // mixing proportions
    real mu[K];       // locations of mixture components
    real<lower=0,upper=10> sigma[K]; // scales of mixture components
  }
  model {
    real ps[K]; // temp for log component densities
    for (k in 1:K) {
      mu[k] ~ normal(0,10);
    }
    for (n in 1:N) {
      for (k in 1:K) {
        ps[k] <- log(theta[k]) + normal_log(y[n],mu[k],sigma[k]);
      }
      increment_log_prob(log_sum_exp(ps));
    }
  }'
# prepare the data - a mixture of Normal(-1,2), Normal (3,1)
# with proportion theta = (0.3, 0.7) respectively
Ndata <- 500 # total number of data points
aprop <- 0.3
bprop <- 1 - aprop
aN <- round(Ndata * aprop)
bN <- Ndata - aN
A <- rnorm(aN, -1, 2)
B <- rnorm(bN, 3, 1)
data <- c(A, B)
library(ggplot2) # in case it isn't mentioned earlier
qplot(data, geom='histogram')
# now convert this into Stan friendly format
stan_data <- list(K=2, N=Ndata, y=data)

set_cppo('fast')
fit <- stan(model_code=lpmodel, data=stan_data, iter = 1000, chains = 4)
print(fit)
plot(fit)
traceplot(fit)

As can be seen in the attached knitr'd pdf file, the chains appear to converge to two different modes (am I imagining things?).  The parameters do appear to be recovered - but not in a simple fashion as the chains cannot be merged or can they?

What happens next in the analysis? How are these multiple modes normally handled?

In my analysis I expect to have a mixture of about 20 reasonably distinct Gaussians - can I expect to get 20 modes?

Your thoughts on this will be appreciated.

Kind regards,

Sean O'Riordain
Trinity College,
Dublin

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Mixture modelling and multiple modes.
messages.body_plain:
Are the two distinct modes just swapping indices?  We talk
about that in the manual.  See also the section on problematic
models.

Inferences that don't depend on indexe identifiers are fine
with multiple chains.

It's just that there's no way to use the convergence diagnostics
because each chain doesn't mix across modes.

Unfortunately, the problem is worse than multiplicative.
With 20 indices you get 20! modes.

What many people tend to do in practice is just use inference
from a single long-running chain.   But you may want to
run multiple chains just to make sure they're getting into
the same neighborhood on log probbability (lp__ "parameter"
in the output).

- Bob

I second Bob's advice, but if you insist on using CmdStan and using R only for analysis, you can easily read the output files as csv files with '#' as a comment character. For example, this will provide a histogram and summary statistics about the theta parameter:

samples <- read.csv('output.csv', comment.char='#')

summary(samples$theta)

If you're using RStan, you can also read in the output files using the read_stan_csv() function.

Daniel

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

Really enjoying RStan, and have a general question about collecting more samples for a pre-existing stanfit object (RStan 2.2.0). The Stanfit object has Rhat values between 1.0 and 1.1, but it looks like the n_effs are a bit low (<100) for some parameters and the CODA raftery diagnostic also suggested more samples would be needed. So basically I just want to collect a few more samples, but using the same model and the same chains (picking up right where the stanfit object had left off and just collecting a few more iterations).

I tried to do this with the code below adapted from the rstan website (https://github.com/stan-dev/rstan/wiki/RStan-Getting-Started#prerequisites).

Newfit <- stan(fit = oldfit, data=data, iter=4500, chains =3)

The first couple of times I tried to run it I got the warning Informational Messages (but over and over again until it crashed). I thought those only applied to convergence and the model had already converged, so I'm a bit confused why those would occur. On one attempt I did get it to run but:

1. The n_effs went down (many to 2!)
2. The Rhat values went up (to values like 13)
3. I now have 2 separate fit objects (although eventually I would like to combine all of my samples)

Does this mean that with more iterations the model is less convergent? Is there a better way of doing this? I also looked for information in the Stan User's Guide, but didn't find anything about this (maybe I missed it?).

I am running R 2.2.0

Thank you for all of your help.

Adrienne

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] stan and PK modeling
messages.body_plain:
You can just do this directly in Stan.  First
note that the usual linear regression

  y[i] = alpha * x[i] + beta + epsilon[i];
  epsilon[i] ~ normal(0,sigma);

translates into Stan as follows:

  y[i] ~ normal(alpha * x[i] + beta, sigma);

The epsilon[i] term is marginalized out, but you
can recover it as a generated quantity as
(y[i] - (alpha * x[i] + beta)) if you need the residuals
for something.

You can do the same thing with your system, which
I'm writing fully indexed as:

  y[i] = model[i] + (err1[i] * model[i]) + err2[i];

  err1[i] ~ normal(0,sigma1);
  err2[i] ~ normal(0,sigma2);

This becomes

  y[i] ~ normal(model[i] + (err1[i] * model[i]), sigma2);
  err1[i] ~ normal(0, sigma1);

At least I think that works out to what you want.  With
essentially two error terms and one that varies by item, I'm
curious as to how it'll fit.

What priors were you thinking of using for the sigma?

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] collecting more iterations with a Stanfit object
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] collecting more iterations with a Stanfit object
messages.body_plain:
I'm not sure if RStan has a way of restarting, because it
requires reinitializing with the adapted mass matrices (step scales
and optionally rotation) and time intervals (step sizes).  You can
re-use the fit object in RStan to avoid recompiling.

Otherwise, we recommend just fitting more chains and running the
whole thing longer, including warmup, the second time around.  We
decided this would be a reasonable strategy because it's going to
take on the order of twice as long to run twice as many iterations.
That's a total budget of 3 time units (1 initial, 2 followup) as
opposed to running from where you left off, which is (1 initial, 1 followup).

And we definitely recommend running in parallel if you have the cores
available.

We're going to add the restart feature relatively soon --- it's one
our high priority list of features for the interfaces.

- Bob

messages.subject: Would solving linear algebra on GPU (using e.g. ViennaCL) speed up large models?
messages.subject_clean: Would solving linear algebra on GPU (using e.g. ViennaCL) speed up large models?
messages.body_plain:
This question is more just out of curiosity than anything else:

I'm starting to play around with using OpenCL to parallelize C++ code to a GPU. I recently came across the ViennaCL <http://viennacl.sourceforge.net/viennacl-about.html> library which enables parallelizing most basic linear algebra functionality.

It looks like ViennaCL interfaces quite nicely with Eigen <http://viennacl.sourceforge.net/viennacl-examples-eigen.html>, making it easy to copy Eigen objects directly into corresponding ViennaCL objects. And I think that ViennaCL has all the functionality that Stan uses in Eigen, from basic linear algebra to inverses, determinants, eigen values, and even the FFT module. The one exception is I'm not sure if it's a 1:1 match on cholesky decomposition, though ViennaCL does have some cholesky functionality.

So my question for those of you who know Stan's C++ backend better than me is: do you think that large, complicated models (e.g. those with millions of datapoints and tens of thousands of parameters - currently taking several hundred seconds for each NUTS step) might benefit from using something like this? Are there any obvious roadblocks that would make it infeasible?

If there's no glaring reasons to declare it a dead end, I'd like to try implementing a single function (e.g. maybe the Eigen solver of optimization/newton.hpp) in ViennaCL. Granted, a partial implementation will probably actually be significantly slower due to overhead in copying objects back and forth, but it should make for a proof of concept.

Hi Kyle,

On Tue, Mar 25, 2014 at 10:06 PM, Kyle Foreman <kylef...@gmail.com> wrote:

> This question is more just out of curiosity than anything else:

> ...

> So my question for those of you who know Stan's C++ backend better than me is: do you think that large, complicated models (e.g. those with millions of datapoints and tens of thousands of parameters - currently taking several hundred seconds for each NUTS step) might benefit from using something like this? Are there any obvious roadblocks that would make it infeasible?
>

YES. And yes.

Within the developers, we actually don't have too much practical experience in C++ with threading / parallelization. Especially when it comes to cross-platform threading. (We have some experience in the Java world where it's much easier to multi-thread and have it implemented cross-platform.) If there's a way to do it, we'd love to hear about it and help out.

So the biggest roadblock is auto-differentiation. (Bob, if you have a chance, can you help chime in on roadblocks here?) We currently build an expression graph to do reverse-mode auto-diff by propagating the chain rule over the expression graph. I don't know if OpenCL or ViennaCL can handle parallelization over auto-diff. This is where my knowledge falls short and hopefully Bob or Matt or someone else knows how to do this.

> I'm starting to play around with using OpenCL to parallelize C++ code to a GPU. I recently came across the ViennaCL <http://viennacl.sourceforge.net/viennacl-about.html> library which enables parallelizing most basic linear algebra functionality.
>
> It looks like ViennaCL interfaces quite nicely with Eigen <http://viennacl.sourceforge.net/viennacl-examples-eigen.html>, making it easy to copy Eigen objects directly into corresponding ViennaCL objects. And I think that ViennaCL has all the functionality that Stan uses in Eigen, from basic linear algebra to inverses, determinants, eigen values, and even the FFT module. The one exception is I'm not sure if it's a 1:1 match on cholesky decomposition, though ViennaCL does have some cholesky functionality.

The big question mark is can ViennaCL handle auto-diff variables as the first template parameter in Eigen's matrix classes? If so, then it's possible. If not, then we're S.O.L. Something that would be useful is to know what the requirements are for ViennaCL to handle parallelization. If you could provide that to the developers, we could start thinking in that direction and pushing to how we can meet those requirements.

>
> If there's no glaring reasons to declare it a dead end, I'd like to try implementing a single function (e.g. maybe the Eigen solver of optimization/newton.hpp) in ViennaCL. Granted, a partial implementation will probably actually be significantly slower due to overhead in copying objects back and forth, but it should make for a proof of concept.

Definitely no reason to declare it a dead end.

If you're able to demonstrate how to do this, we're more than happy to help extend Stan in that direction. Right now, the dev team has its hands full, so if you wanted help implementing it you might have to wait a bit, but giving guidance is a lot less time intensive and we're able to do that at any time.

Thank you for bringing this up.

Daniel

On Tue, Mar 25, 2014 at 2:32 PM, Adrienne Tucker <atuck...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Thanks Bob, looking forward to another nice feature! In the meantime, would it be possible to obtain an equivalent result by indeed starting over from scratch and running the whole thing longer but recreating the same init values and the same seed values?

If you set the init values and the seeds, you will get the same samples as long as the number of warmup samples is fixed. Just to be concrete about it, if you start with number of warmup samples = 1000 and number of samples = 1000, if you set the number of warmup samples = 1000 and number of samples = 10k, the first 1000 samples will be identical. (If you find that is not true, please let us know and we'll track down the bug.)

With that said, if you went from number of warmup samples = 1000 and number of samples = 1000 to number of warmup samples = 2000 and number of samples = 2000, there's no reason to believe that any of the 2000 samples will be identical to the 1000 samples. Hopefully the inference about the parameters stay the same, but if the model hasn't converged with 1000 samples, you might see different results with 10k samples.

Daniel

matrices, namely that they're usually hard to estimate.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] stan and PK modeling
messages.body_plain:
On 3/26/2014 12:57 PM, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>> Thanks, Bob.  I was planning to use Cauchy (0,5) for sigmas.  Based on examples in stan I understood that it is current best practice.
>>
> It depends on what you know about the scale.  If you
> expect unit normal noise, then it's overly broad, but if
> you expect noise on the scale of 100, it's overly narrow.

I think the noise should be unit normal.  Perhaps it makes sense to try
sigma ~ Uniform (0, 1).

>> Does it make sense to write the model as (no index on err1):
>>    y[i] ~ normal(model[i] + (err1 * model[i]), sigma2);
>>    err1 ~ normal(0, sigma1);
>>
> Yes, you could do that.  Then it's not really noise so much as you
> want (1 + err1) as a multiplier of model[i].  Why would you want this
> rather than just rescaling model directly?

With regards to err1 with index I was concerned that it may not converge.

Yet another question.  PK models often have lags.  It means that nothing
happens until some time t0.  For example, model(t)=0 when t < t0;
model(t)=exp(t-t0)-1 when t>=t0.  As such there is C0 continuity but
gradient is discontinuous at t=t0.  Obviously I want t0 to be a
parameter to estimate.

Linas

> On 3/26/2014 12:57 PM, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>>> Thanks, Bob.  I was planning to use Cauchy (0,5) for sigmas.  Based on examples in stan I understood that it is current best practice.
>>>
>> It depends on what you know about the scale.  If you
>> expect unit normal noise, then it's overly broad, but if
>> you expect noise on the scale of 100, it's overly narrow.
> I think the noise should be unit normal.  Perhaps it makes sense to try sigma ~ Uniform (0, 1).
>>> Does it make sense to write the model as (no index on err1):
>>>   y[i] ~ normal(model[i] + (err1 * model[i]), sigma2);
>>>   err1 ~ normal(0, sigma1);
>>>
>> Yes, you could do that.  Then it's not really noise so much as you
>> want (1 + err1) as a multiplier of model[i].  Why would you want this
>> rather than just rescaling model directly?
> With regards to err1 with index I was concerned that it may not converge.
>

That's a valid concern because you'd get a redundant parameterization.
I just don't think it's doing anything without an index other than
rescaling a bit in a way that's also going to cause a near multiplicative
invariance between all of the model[i] and err1.

> Yet another question.  PK models often have lags.  It means that nothing happens until some time t0.  For example, model(t)=0 when t < t0; model(t)=exp(t-t0)-1 when t>=t0.  As such there is C0 continuity but gradient is discontinuous at t=t0.  Obviously I want t0 to be a parameter to estimate.

I don't think model(t) as written is discontinuous at t0.

But in general, you can give particular data points different models.
For instance, in a time series, the first point can get a diffuse
prior, the next point one based on just a single previous point and
so on up to the general loop.

- Bob

messages.subject: pD for DIC
messages.body_plain:
Hi all

I have a doubt related to how to calculate properly the DIC. In BDA 3 in page 172 - 173 explains the calculation of the dice, which includes the deviance and the pD (the effective number of parameters). My concern is about the pD. BDA mentions 2 ways to calculate it, the first is how i have seen it in many articles, the second one BDA explains it is also valid but it doesnt explain it extensively.

The first one is
pD = Dbar -  Dhat

The second one is
pDalt = 2 variance(log-likelihood)

Could someone help me understand the similarities between these 2 calculations and the differences? Or guide to a articles that exaplains it more extensively (since i havent been able to find one)?

I also found that jags gives the first method mentioned here and a third method propose by Martyn Plummer (Penalized loss functions for Bayesian model comparison, 2008), and these can be obtain using the r package rjags, but using the package R2jags, it only gives the DIC using the pDalt.

Given that there are other information criteria that are based on the deviance, and the difference is in the penalized (pD), like AIC and BIC, using different pD's to calculate the DIC would give three different DIC's, and these three DIC's should not be consider the same, but different information criteria?

Thanks for any help

 - Mauricio

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] pD for DIC
messages.body_plain:
The information criteria aren’t independent — they actually follow a pretty rigid criteria,

evidence -> BIC

cross validation -> WAIC -> DIC -> AIC

where “->” denotes further approximations.  So WAIC and DIC don’t have different approximations
in as much as DIC has more approximations than WAIC.

For more see http://projecteuclid.org/euclid.ssu/1356628931 and http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/research/published/waic_understand3.pdf.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Multiple imputations and stan
messages.body_plain:
I'm not sure about the best way to do multiple imputation, but
we're interested in doing this in Stan.

The approach you're suggesting (use a random subset of imputed data
in each iteration) is a more stochastic data approach
that's related to other issues like "cut" in BUGS that have been
brought up before.  I'm not sure it's ideal computationally because
of the interaction with adaptation.

I'm not even sure the approach you suggest produces the same posterior
as what Ben was suggesting (fit a bunch of random subsets, then pool
chains).

Adding auxiliary variables that don't affect the likelihood is
not a problem --- they just marginalize out as you'd expect in
the inferences.  HMC itself takes the parameter vector theta and
adds an auxiliary variable of the same size consisting of
momentum/kinetic energy terms.  The momentum terms are then marginalized
out for inference (Stan users don't even see them).

- Bob

On Mar 28, 2014, at 10:29 AM, Guido Biele <guido...@gmail.com> wrote:

>
> Multiple imputation
> Hello,
> I need to run regressions with imputed data and would like to hear your opinion about which method you think I should use.
> Background: I am working with a relatively large dataset (N is up to 50000) on which I run regressions with typically 5-15 variables of interest. The data set has many more variables which I can use in the imputation process. Variables can be continuous, ordered factor, or binary). Data are certainly not missing completely at random*. Only around 25% of the cases have missing data.
> My first Idea was to do imputation and estimation of the regression model of interest in the same stan model. I did a simple test with simulated data which worked fine (see code below), but while doing the test I realized that scaling this to my own dataset would be extremely time-consuming.
>
> The alternative then is to do the imputation first (e.g. with mi) and to do the final regression model in stan. Here, Ben proposed in an earlier post to
>  (a) run the stan model repeatedly with the different versions of the imputed data sets and
>  (b) merge the chains from these models
> I’d like to hear your opinion about an alternative way to use the different versions of the imputed data sets:
>  (a) submit the originally complete part of the dataset and different versions of the imputed data to the same model and
>  (b) specify the model such that likelihood is computed for the originally completed data plus a randomly chosen imputed data set
> Specifically, when
> Ycomp      =        criterion values for complete data
> Yimp       =        criterion values for imputed data
> Xcomp      =        design matrix for complete data
> Xsimp      =        array with design matrices for imputed data
> alpha      =        intercept parameter
> beta       =        vector of regression weights
> sigma      =        regression error
>
> the crucial part of the model specification would be:
> Y ~ normal( Xcomp * beta, sigma)
> Ycomp ~ normal(Xsimp [k] *  beta, sigma)  // where k is a random number
>
> It seems to me, this would be more efficient than running multiple stan models on different imputed data sets, when only (in my case) ca. 25% of the cases would differ between imputed data sets. Does this make sense?
> If yes, the problem to solve would be to get the random number k. in stan, random numbers can only be generated in the “generated quantities block”. Hence, would this (I fear) trick work:
> First I specify a parameter _k with an (implicit) uniform prior in the parameters block:
> real<lower=0,upper=impN> real_k;  // impN = number of versions of imputed data
> Then I convert it to an integer in the model block (following a proposal from Bob in another post):
> int k;
>     k <- 1;
>     while ((k + 1) < floor(real_k))
>       k <- k + 1;
>
> I have a bad feeling about specifying a parameter that will be updated even though it has no influence on the likelihood (I don’t know enough about the sampler to know if this is problematic ), but I don’t have a better solution at the moment.
>
> Sorry for the long post.
> Looking forward to you feedback
> Guido
>
>
>
> *The data set includes for example children’s birth weight and their mothers’ response to questions about smoking. Not surprisingly, mothers who did not provide smoking information have on average lighter children.
>
> #############################################################################
> ####################### test simple imputation model in R #########################
> #############################################################################
>
> library(stan)
>
> ####################### make data set #########################
> nobs = 2500
>
> M = matrix(c(1, 0.4, 0.6, 0.6,
>              0.4, 1, 0.3, 0.94,
>              0.6, 0.3, 1, 0.2,
>              0.6, 0.94, 0.2, 1), nrow=4, ncol=4)
>
> # Cholesky decomposition
> L = chol(M)
> nvars = dim(L)[1]
>
> # Random variables that follow an M correlation matrix
> r = t(L) %*% matrix(rnorm(nvars*nobs,sd = .5), nrow=nvars, ncol=nobs)
> r = t(r)
>
> rdata = data.frame(r)
> names(rdata) = c('r', 'p1', 'p2', 'p3')
> Y = r[,1]
> X = r[,2:4]
>
> nvars = 3
> nmissings = round(nobs*.25/nvars)*nvars
> missings = matrix(sample(nobs,nmissings),ncol = nvars)
> complete = seq(nobs)[-missings]
> nms =
>
> ####################### put data together for stan #########################
> standata = list(Y = Y,
>                 X = X,
>                 N = nobs,
>                 Ncomp = length(complete),
>                 compIDX = complete,
>                 Nmis1 = nrow(missings),
>                 Nmis2 = nrow(missings),
>                 Nmis3 = nrow(missings),
>                 mis1IDX = missings[,1],
>                 mis2IDX = missings[,2],
>                 mis3IDX = missings[,3]
>   )
>
>
> ############################  stan model ##############################
> modelcode = "
> data {
>   int<lower=0> N;                   // number of complete data
>   vector[N] Y;                      // vector with outcome
>   matrix[N,3] X;                    // design matrix (predictors)
>   int<lower=0> Ncomp;
>   int<lower=0> compIDX[Ncomp];
>   int<lower=0> Nmis1;
>   int<lower=0> Nmis2;
>   int<lower=0> Nmis3;
>   int<lower=0> mis1IDX[Nmis1];
>   int<lower=0> mis2IDX[Nmis2];
>   int<lower=0> mis3IDX[Nmis3];
> }
>
> parameters {
>   vector[3] beta;                   // regression weight fro ultimate predictors
>   real<lower=0> sigma_Y;            // error term for ultimate regression
>   vector[2] beta_imp1;              // regression weights to impute missing variables 1-3
>   vector[2] beta_imp2;
>   vector[2] beta_imp3;
>   real<lower=0> sigma_imp1;         // error terms for imputation of missing variables 1-3
>   real<lower=0> sigma_imp2;
>   real<lower=0> sigma_imp3;
> }
>
> model {
>   matrix[N,3] compX;
>   int idx;
>
>   compX <- rep_matrix(1,N, 3);      // prepare design matrix to be filled with imputed data
>   compX <- compX .* X;
>
>   beta ~ cauchy(0,2.5);             // using cauchy priors following Gelman et al 2008
>   beta_imp1 ~ cauchy(0,2.5);
>   beta_imp2 ~ cauchy(0,2.5);
>   beta_imp3 ~ cauchy(0,2.5);
>   sigma_Y ~ cauchy(0,2.5);
>   sigma_imp1 ~ cauchy(0,2.5);
>   sigma_imp2 ~ cauchy(0,2.5);
>   sigma_imp3 ~ cauchy(0,2.5);
>
>
>   for (n in 1:Ncomp){               // regression weights for imputations
>     idx <-  compIDX[n];
>     X[idx,1] ~ normal(beta_imp1[1] * X[idx,2] + beta_imp1[2] * X[idx,3], sigma_imp1);
>     X[idx,2] ~ normal(beta_imp2[1] * X[idx,1] + beta_imp2[2] * X[idx,3], sigma_imp2);
>     X[idx,3] ~ normal(beta_imp3[1] * X[idx,1] + beta_imp3[2] * X[idx,2], sigma_imp3);
>   }
>
>
>   for (k in 1:Nmis1){               // impute missing data
>     idx <- mis1IDX[k];
>     compX[idx,1] <- beta_imp1[1] * X[idx,2] + beta_imp1[2] * X[idx,3];}
>   for (l in 1:Nmis2){
>     idx <- mis2IDX[l];
>     compX[idx,2] <- beta_imp2[1] * X[idx,1] + beta_imp2[2] * X[idx,3];}
>   for (m in 1:Nmis3){
>     idx <- mis3IDX[m];
>     compX[idx,3] <- beta_imp3[1] * X[idx,1] + beta_imp3[2] * X[idx,2];}
>
>   Y  ~  normal(compX  * beta, sigma_Y);
> }
>
> "
> ############################  run stan model ##############################
> stan_imp = stan(model_name="test_imp", model_code = modelcode, data=standata ,  iter = 5000, chains = 4,seed = 12345)
>
>

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] assigning to sub vectors
messages.body_plain:
Not yet.  The only expressions allowed on the LHS
of an assignment are a variable and optional indices.

In programming language terms, none of the Stan functions produce
lvalues as output within Stan.  The only operation that produces
lvalues is indexing a variable.

In the C++ implementation, most functions also do not produce
valid C++ lvalues because of the way Eigen's expression templates
work and our simplified return typing.  Because we declare functions
to return Matrix<T,R,C> instances, this causes a copy on return for
any intermediate expression templates.  We'll soon be rewriting some of the
matrix auto-diff to take advantage of the expression templates from
Eigen, which has shown some substantial speedups in early prototypes
for matrix functions (factors of 3 or so!).  This will in turn make it
easier to have more elaborate lvalues in the Stan language.

I also hope to implement the full R-like array indexing, so you
can write things like:

   a[1:3] <- b;

   c <- d[1:3,];

   e <- f[2:9,13:101];

Probably some time over the next year :-)

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] stan and PK modeling
messages.body_plain:
I'm not sure what you mean by a reference --- my understanding
is that it's common practice in time-series models.

If you have a time series of data points y[1],...,y[N],
and you want to in general model y[n] as a function of
y[n-1], y[n-2], ..., y[n-K], then you have to have a different
model for y[1],...y[K], because you don't have the relevant
predictors.

- Bob

>>> Yet another question.  PK models often have lags.  It means that nothing happens until some time t0.  For example, model(t)=0 when t < t0; model(t)=exp(t-t0)-1 when t>=t0.  As such there is C0 continuity but gradient is discontinuous at t=t0.  Obviously I want t0 to be a parameter to estimate.
>> I don't think model(t) as written is discontinuous at t0.
>>
>> But in general, you can give particular data points different models.
>> For instance, in a time series, the first point can get a diffuse
>> prior, the next point one based on just a single previous point and

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Multiple imputations and stan
messages.body_plain:
Thanks for your quick response Bob,

I want to clarify one thing because I did not want to propose to fit a random subset of the imputed data, at least not if subset means using only a subset of the cases for which imputation was done.

Let’s say we have a dataset with 900 complete and 100 incomplete cases with missing data. Then we perform multiple imputations to get imputed 5 data sets, each consisting of the 900 originally complete cases plus 100 cases with imputation of missing data (with some variation in imputation values between the 5 imputed data sets).

Ben’s suggestion was to fit the 5 datasets (1000 cases each) in independent stan calls and then to merge the chains.

My proposal was to make one stan call to which I submit 900 complete cases plus 5 versions of 100 cases with imputations. For the likelihood calculation I would then each time use all 900 originally complete cases plus one of the 5 sets (randomly chosen) of 100 cases with imputed data.

I understand the potential problem during the adaptation (of sampling parameters I assume). Still, I think this is not necessarily a problem because the imputed values should be similar across imputation versions.

I guess I’ll give it a try and report back.

Cheers - Guido

messages.subject: Re: Multiple imputations and stan
messages.body_plain:
On Friday, March 28, 2014 5:29:54 AM UTC-4, Guido Biele wrote:
> My first Idea was to do imputation and estimation of the regression model of interest in the same stan model. I did a simple test with simulated data which worked fine (see code below), but while doing the test I realized that scaling this to my own dataset would be extremely time-consuming.

That is the best way, but it wouldn't work in Stan if there were missingness on the discrete variables. So, you will probably have to impute first.

> The alternative then is to do the imputation first (e.g. with mi) and to do the final regression model in stan. Here, Ben proposed in an earlier post to
>  (a) run the stan model repeatedly with the different versions of the imputed data sets and
>  (b) merge the chains from these models
> I’d like to hear your opinion about an alternative way to use the different versions of the imputed data sets:
>  (a) submit the originally complete part of the dataset and different versions of the imputed data to the same model and
>  (b) specify the model such that likelihood is computed for the originally completed data plus a randomly chosen imputed data set

I think if you were to go this route it would be (in the same model) do the complete part and all the imputed parts giving them each a fixed weight of 1/m.

> Specifically, when
> Ycomp      =        criterion values for complete data
> Yimp       =        criterion values for imputed data
> Xcomp      =        design matrix for complete data
> Xsimp      =        array with design matrices for imputed data
> alpha      =        intercept parameter
> beta       =        vector of regression weights
> sigma      =        regression error
>
> the crucial part of the model specification would be:
> Y ~ normal( Xcomp * beta, sigma)
> Ycomp ~ normal(Xsimp [k] *  beta, sigma)  // where k is a random number
>
> It seems to me, this would be more efficient than running multiple stan models on different imputed data sets, when only (in my case) ca. 25% of the cases would differ between imputed data sets. Does this make sense?
> If yes, the problem to solve would be to get the random number k. in stan, random numbers can only be generated in the “generated quantities block”. Hence, would this (I fear) trick work:
> First I specify a parameter _k with an (implicit) uniform prior in the parameters block:
> real<lower=0,upper=impN> real_k;  // impN = number of versions of imputed data
> Then I convert it to an integer in the model block (following a proposal from Bob in another post):
> int k;
>     k <- 1;
>     while ((k + 1) < floor(real_k))
>       k <- k + 1;
>
> I have a bad feeling about specifying a parameter that will be updated even though it has no influence on the likelihood (I don’t know enough about the sampler to know if this is problematic ), but I don’t have a better solution at the moment.

We have never been able to be too optimistic about these ideas that discretize a continuous parameter. Most likely, the chain would get stuck on the same imputed part for long stretches at a time. I think explicit averaging over the imputed parts would work better than implicit averaging by choosing each imputed part with probability 1/m.

Ben

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: How to interpret lp__?
messages.body_plain:
It depends on how you write the model.  Suppose you have
data y and parameters vector.  exp(lp__) is proportional
to p(theta|y).

In practice, if you only use sampling statements (~), lp__
will be the log joint, log p(y,theta), less any constant
terms that only depend on y.

If you use increment_log_prob(normal(log(x,mu,sigma)), then
you don't drop normalizing terms compared to x ~ normal(mu,sigma);.
But they sample over the same posterior.

- Bob

Good point.  These two need Jacobians:

In both cases, it's a sqrt(x) transform.  But we just tend to use the

As to transforming sigma, that was popular for BUGS because it used
a precision parameterization (1/sigma^2)
and people often care about the scale (sigma).

messages.body_plain:
On Saturday, March 29, 2014 8:48:42 PM UTC-4, Avraham Adler wrote:
> If you note my original post, I fixed the name.
>
> And Dr. Goodrich, I apologize profusely for not originally ascribing credit properly.

Not a big deal. The real credit should go to Lewandowski, Kurowicka, and Joe but Bob and I have long since given up on being able to spell all that (hence the LKJ).

Anyway, the broader point here is that calculating a matrix decomposition of a parameterized matrix in Stan is expensive, in part because the number of operations depends on the cube of the number of rows and in part because Stan has to use its auto-diff mechanism to compute the derivatives (which involves a chain rule whose number of links also depends on the cube of the number of rows) with respect to each scalar parameter. So if you do something like

cholesky_decompose( diag_matrix(scales) * correlation_matrix * diag_matrix(scales) )

or

cholesky decompose( variance * correlation matrix )

the cholesky_decompose() function just sees a square matrix and does not recognize that these are equivalent to

diag_matrix(scales) * cholesky_decompose(correlation_matrix)

and

sqrt(variance) * choleksy_decompose(correlation_matrix)

respectively (although as Philippe pointed out, this particular trick only applies with a diagonal matrix or a scalar).

However, you ultimately want something equivalent which does not entail taking an expensive Cholesky decomposition of a correlation matrix. The attachment constructs and L such that L * L' is a correlation matrix that is distributed LKJ with shape parameter eta. So, if you use that, then the above expressions are equivalent to

diag_matrix(scales) * L

and

sqrt(variance) * L

But wait, there's more! If something is getting a multivariate normal prior (or more generally anything in the elliptical distribution family), then you don't want to actually use of the multi_normal functions (ideally, those should only be used for likelihoods of data). You can make Pars a local or transformed parameter that is a function of the primitive parameter vector z via the multivariate Matt trick:

z ~ normal(0,1);

This way avoids having to solve a triangular system of equations inside one of the multi_normal functions. All that said, none of this makes much difference when dealing with a 2x2 covariance matrix, but it is much better when the dimension of the covariance matrix is large.

Ben

A few general points. I cannot think of a reason why anyone should ever call one of the multi_normal functions when the thing to the left of the ~ is a parameter. Instead, you should either
Use the stochastic representation and multivariate Matt trick (beta <- mu + L * z where z ~ normal(0,1) and L is the Cholesky factor of the covariance matrix)
Use direct incrementation of the log-posterior with calls to increment_log_prob()
Use the univariate normal density when the covariance matrix is diagonal
As it applies to your situation,
You won't need to create the vector of zeros in the transformed parameter block, however ...
You should definitely construct the constant matrix L_sre <- cholesky_decompose(spd_inverse(Ones - phi * H)*Delta) inside the transformed parameters block
Substitute beta1_z for beta1 in the parameters block and write this in the model block beta1 <- sqrt(tau_sq) * (L_sre * beta1_z)
Also, in the model block do beta2 ~ normal(0, sqrt(sigma_sq))
Ben

On Mar 31, 2014, at 9:20 AM, MT <micha...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Specifically, I have the lingering confusion of when and how to use increment_log_prob correctly.
> This was one of the reasons I wanted to shy away from it, mostly due to my lack of familiarity.
>
> Reading the documentation, it says increment_log_prob can be useful for two general purposes
>
> 1) when one wishes to sample after a change of variables (making note that lp_ is not needed for transformations)
> 2) for custom distributions eg triangle dist.
>

The basic idea is that lp__ is the variable in which the total
log probability returned by the model is manipulated.  A sampling
statement:

   y ~ foo(theta);

is equivalent in terms of sampling to

  increment_log_prob(foo_log(y,theta));

and also to

  lp__ <- lp__ + foo_log(y,theta);

though direct manipulation of lp__ is deprecated (we'll eventually
remove it).  The point of a Stan model is to specify the log probability
function and the sampling statements are just syntactic sugar plus an
optimization that drops constant terms (and is hence a bit more efficient
where available than incrementing with the _log function).

Yes, we need to fix the symmetry tests. And we need to add more data
types (e.g., Cholesky factor for correlation matrix) and
multivariate distributions (e.g., the LKJ density over such factors)
so that we can efficiently use the sampling notation.

What you want to compare is not so much time to 1000 iterations
as time to convergence and number of effective samples per second
after convergence.  JAGS/BUGS/Stan may run fast per iteration in some
models but have low numbers of effective samples per iteration.  Suggestions
like reparameterizing (different strategies for Gibbs vs. HMC) often
speed up effective samples per iteration, not speed per iteration.

- Bob

On Mar 30, 2014, at 6:07 PM, Ben Goodrich <goodri...@gmail.com> wrote:

> On Saturday, March 29, 2014 8:48:42 PM UTC-4, Avraham Adler wrote:

>

I think Ben's being too modest here.  He figured out both how to implement
the LKJ model using matrix operations and how to use it for applied
modeling.  See:

http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/research/unpublished/Visualization.pdf

which has nice comparisons to (inverse) Wishart.  It's changed the way
we think about modeling covariance matrices --- instead of scaled (inverse)
Wisharts, as recommended in Andrew's books, we now favor a scaled
correlation matrix with an LKJ prior.  Too bad Andrew couldn't have snuck
it into the 3rd Edition of Bayesian Data Analysis --- it'll definitely be
in the 2nd Edition of Gelman and Hill :-)

- Bob

On Mar 29, 2014, at 9:09 PM, Joshua Wiley <jwiley...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Dear Herra and Bob,
>
> Thank you very much for the tips.  Yes, the transforms were left over from BUGS and working with precisions instead of scale (plus I ran across one Stan example online doing it).
>
> Dropping the transform and just using sigma's directly seems to be helping some.  Much appreciated!
>
> I am familiar with the concept of vectorizing form R, although I do not quite get yet where all in Stan I can and cannot, so thank you as well for the example code of the pieces I can vectorize.

We have just begun to vectorize the basic functions.  But all
of the univariate densities are vectorized on all of their arguments.
(But so far, it doesn't play nicely with truncation.)

> Under various simulations, the model is running pretty well now after the first couple hundred warmup iterations, which makes me think it is a starting values issue.  My hunch is that it is most likely an issue related to the residual variances, so I am thinking about passing start values based on the raw values (i.e., rather than use a hierarchical model, just have R calculate SDs by ID, and get the shape and rate parameters of the gamma as mean^2 / variance and mean/variance).

This can help, but usually if there's a model that takes a few
hundred warmup iterations to converge it's often a problem with
too-broad priors.  Stan's very good at exploring broad swaths of
the posterior, whereas BUGS/JAGS will appear to be better behaved
because they won't properly sample from the posterior.  You can
diagnose by looking at the widths of posterior intervals or posterior sd.
In that case, tighter priors help control inference.

> I'll post back how things go.

Posting back would be great.

> Cheers,
>
> Josh
>
> P.S. I saw in the FAQ that a collection of example models might be being made, happy for this to be included under a CC-BY license.

Even better.  Thanks.

- Bob

>                 sigma_a * sigma_a);
>             concentration [t] ~ normal (model_c, sigma);
>         }
>
> However for some combination of parameters model_c is negative as well as concentration.  When using explicit likelihood function I assign very low number to the likelihood whenever model_c<0 - don't know if it is a good practice but basically I tell the solver not to explore infeasible set of  parameters.  How to do this in stan?

Priors on B1, B2, B3 would be the way to go, or even hard constraints
making them positive if that makes sense for the model.  Or equivalently,
putting them inside the exp() function as additive terms.

There's a square(x) function, by the way, which is a bit more
efficient than x * x.   (And we really need to add normal distributions
parameterized with variance and precision, which would avoid that
sqrt operation, too --- it's just going to get squared again inside
the density!).

You could also constrain concentration to be positive, though you'll
still get odd behavior with model_c going below 0 (it's symmetric around
0 in the sigma term).

Could you write back with exactly what you're trying to do and the
full model?  traceplot only works for quantities declared as parameters,
transformed parameters, or generated quantities.

messages.body_plain:
Dear Community,
I am trying to run the example model for a multivariate (hierarchical) regression on page 95 of the Reference Manual for Stan version 2.2.0 but I am running into a compiling error.

This is the error message returned when calling stan():

TRANSLATING MODEL 'fullmodel' FROM Stan CODE TO C++ CODE NOW.
Error in stanc(file = file, model_code = model_code, model_name = model_name,  :
  failed to parse Stan model 'fullmodel' with error message:
EXPECTATION FAILURE LOCATION: file=input; line=27, column=57

beta[j] ~ multi_normal((u[j] * gamma)’, Sigma_beta);
                                                        ^-- here
DIAGNOSTIC(S) FROM PARSER:
no matches for function name="multi_normal_log"
    arg 0 type=vector
    arg 1 type=row vector
    arg 2 type=matrix
available function signatures for multi_normal_log:
0.  multi_normal_log(vector, vector, matrix) : real
unknown distribution=multi_normal
Parser expecting: <eps>

I have actually slightly modified the code to fit a logistic rather than a linear model but I doubt this is the problem. Here is the modified code (note commented out lines):
fullmodel<- '
data {
int<lower=0> N; // num individuals
int<lower=1> K; // num ind predictors
int<lower=1> J; // num groups
int<lower=1> L; // num group predictors
int<lower=1,upper=J> jj[N]; // group for individual
matrix[N,K] x; // individual predictors
matrix[J,L] u; // group predictors
vector[N] y; // outcomes
}
parameters {
corr_matrix[K] Omega; // prior covariance
vector<lower=0>[K] tau; // prior scale
matrix[L,K] gamma; // group coeffs
vector[K] beta[J]; // indiv coeffs by group
#real<lower=0> sigma; // prediction error scale of the original linear model (commented out)
}
model {
matrix[K,K] Sigma_beta;
Sigma_beta <- diag_matrix(tau) * Omega * diag_matrix(tau);
tau ~ cauchy(0,2.5);
Omega ~ lkj_corr(2);
for (l in 1:L)
gamma[l] ~ normal(0,5);
for (j in 1:J)
beta[j] ~ multi_normal((u[j] * gamma)’, Sigma_beta);
for (n in 1:N)
#y[n] ~ normal(x[n] * beta[jj[n]], sigma); // original linear predictor commented out
y[n] ~ bernoulli(inv_logit(x[n] * beta[jj[n]]));
}
'
I am using R version 3.0.2 (2013-09-25) in Platform: x86_64-w64-mingw32/x64 (64-bit) and rstan_2.2.0.
Info on the compiler is:
> system("g++ --version")
G__~1.EXE (GCC) 4.6.3 20111208 (prerelease)

Is this really an error in the manual? Or what can I be doing wrong?
Thanks for any guidance.
Edwin
P.S. Explanations for beginners are highly appreciated.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: "BYM" Spatial Car Model: Slow Sampling (relative to BUGS) + non-symmetric warnings + avoid lp_
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Re: "BYM" Spatial Car Model: Slow Sampling (relative to BUGS) + non-symmetric warnings + avoid lp_
messages.body_plain:
I've successfully run 2100 spatial units with the sparse method - it still takes a while to sample, but it's significantly faster than using multi_normal_prec() for my use case. Results will vary depending on sparsity etc of course. And as Bob notes, it's the effective sample size that's important, not the number of iterations. I find that with these tweaks I get better convergence and much lower time per effective sample than BUGS/JAGS.

I've attached a little tutorial on how to use increment_log_prob() to sample the sparse matrix. It uses the same GeoBUGS Scotland lip cancer example as my original CAR thread. It's pretty thoroughly documented, so hopefully you can get the gist just by reading through.

One sacrifice it makes is that it uses an estimate of the log determinant of the precision matrix instead of computing it directly. To scale it up beyond the 56 spatial units in the example, I recommend sampling the log determinant in R instead of Stan, because that step (which fortunately only has to happen once) is a couple orders of magnitude slower in Stan than R and can take quite a while once you're up to hundreds or thousands of spatial units.

There may be some tricks to replicate the CAR distribution using something like the multivariate Matt trick that Ben mentions - I haven't tried that, but would be very interested to hear how it works if you test it out.

Agreed that a built in distribution would be easier, but before that becomes feasible in a case like this I would think a sparse matrix object for Stan would be required.
